essays.title: Muse
essays.body:
Dead Muddiness Markup

_It might be considered strange_, at the dawn of the AI age, that badly written language takes on it's own charm and is appreciated in a whole new light.

Not as previous good writing was appreciated, original human construction is the new gold surely.

But as the cannibalised slop becomes more ubiquitous, artificial intelligence generated language is to our whole corpus of literature, a virus, a mutation, at first seen as 'efficient', 'empowering' and 'useful' perhaps, but along for the ride is a stinging, insidious, deleterious effect not just on the literature itself, but much more importantly, on the human capacity to produce anything untainted by it.

It's erosive quality when blended into everything else is no more damningly evident than when we look to the wellspring of all literature itself, the human capacity to think, reflect, conceive and feel in human ways.

When all we have done before becomes the engine that produces its own fuel, history holds warning for us that we ignore at our own peril.

essays.title: That was the year that was!
essays.body:
I look back at last year and I do not see a bad patch or a rough season. I see myself fucking my life up in slow motion. I see self-destruction. I see damage I caused, damage I let happen, and damage I did not stop when I still maybe could have. Now I am sitting here in April, far enough away from it to see the shape of the year, and the shape of it is ugly. It is collapse. It is waste. It is me helping to tear through things that were precious to me and then being left to stare at the ruins.

What hits me hardest is the sense of erasure. It feels like I wiped out huge parts of my own life. Not just plans or hopes, but the living parts of it. The human parts. Connection, trust, belonging, steadiness, dignity, friendship, a sense of being someone. So much of that now feels gone or poisoned or too far away to touch. I feel like I have been stripped down to this scared, isolated, ashamed version of myself, and I do not know what to do with the fact that this is where I have ended up.

I am deeply, bitterly sad. Not in some soft or noble way. In a dark, humiliating way. The kind of sadness that sits in the body like rot. The kind that makes you look back and cringe at yourself, recoil from yourself, and feel sick at what you became and what you did and what you failed to protect. There is regret in this, but it is not tidy regret. It is vicious. It is the kind that keeps circling back and saying: you knew better, you should have done better, look what you have done, look what it cost.

And there is no comfort in telling myself it was all just circumstances. That would be a lie. I was part of it. That is what makes it so hard to live with. I can see my own hand in my undoing. I can see moments where I acted badly, failed badly, let myself down, let other people down, gave in to the worst parts of myself, and kept moving in the wrong direction. I do not get to stand outside it as some innocent bystander. I was in it. I was one of the causes. That truth lands like a hammer.

Now I feel lonely in a way that is hard to explain. Not just alone, but cut off. Friendless. Exposed. Ashamed. Like I am living outside the life I was supposed to have, outside the person I thought I was, outside the ordinary human world where people still feel connected and wanted and intact. I feel scared because I do not think this is the sort of damage that clears in a few weeks or a few months. I think I am going to be living with the consequences for years. Maybe that is what frightens me most. Not just that I lost so much, but that I have to go on from here carrying it.

And I hate that this is my reality now. I hate the waste of it. I hate the damage. I hate the shame of knowing that some of this was self-inflicted. I hate how small and erased I feel. I hate that when I look at my life, what I mostly feel is grief and regret and fear. There are things that were precious to me, and I fucked them up or let them die or drove them away, and now I am left with this bleak aftermath and no honest way to pretend it is anything else.

This is not a lesson or character-building,it's just sorrow, regret, loneliness, and the sickening knowledge that I made most of this mess.  Now I have to live inside the consequences of it. That is what the year last was and is forever more now.

essays.title: Dan draft

Dan, I promised a fuller update. Like most of the world, I guess, things have been a little uncertain of late. I actually had a pretty disastrous series of events in 2025 that has set me back some. Nothing to report in terms of a permanent setback like death or disease, more like my old-style self-destruct stuff. I lost my job around July, in very unfair and traumatic circumstances but not wholly uncontributed to by me—I’d say 60-40, the unfairs have it, the unfairs have it! But it was one of those "you and the world are not quite what you thought you were" moments; very disconcerting. I don’t know, my friend, I’ve always had a me-centric view, a selfish view of the world, and a sometimes elevated view of my talents, but I also have a trust and instinct in the goodness of others that I can’t shake, and both bit me hard on this occasion.

Oh well, move on I thought—and in true Clark style, not content with the cluster-fudge of the half-year gone—I outdid myself in the worst possible way. The trauma and emotion of losing my job left me feeling cut down, and so I did what I have always done—saw the big red "DON’T PUSH THIS" button, and pushed it hard. Too awful to share details, Dan, but know I’ve never been closer to truly ending it than I was at the end of 2025.

Self-evidently I didn't, of course; I wouldn't I think, I hope. And now, 10k in psychologist fees later, I am at least stable at the moment, but it’s rocked me very hard fella. I continue to sense and feel a right not to exist even if the strong urge not to has left me.  Not fishing for return arguments on this one,  I am safe and well for the foreseeable in the literal sense so need to attempt counter argument or express concern here mate,  just sharing my inner darkness with one of the last people on earth I have an enduring sense of trust in.  

On the brighter side of this,  I think I managed to get through this without dragging the kids or Moira too far into it - I mean that to convey they were not subject or objects in or to the drama, so apart from the obvious downer that is living with a chronic and clinically depressed suicidal husband for a time,  Moira didn't suffer and is well as the kids, who flew the nest a while back - so were not aware of most of the drama.

essays.title: Spike Strips are now legacy tools
essays.body:
NZ Police Replace Spike Strips With LED ‘Inspiration Road Strips.

WELLINGTON — NZ Police have officially replaced traditional spike strips with a new roadside intervention system featuring flashing LED “Inspiration Road Strips”, designed to encourage drivers to stop through positive messaging rather than tyre deflation.  The new devices, deployed during pursuit situations, project calming affirmations across the roadway such as:

“Stop — You Are Enough”

“You Are Safe To Slow Down”

“This Moment Does Not Define You”

“Consider Pulling Over For Your Own Wellbeing”

Police say the change reflects a move away from “old-school, unpredictable outcomes” associated with spike strips, which physically disable vehicles.

Police spokesperson Colin Dekops said the upgrade is about modernising the tone of roadside interventions.
“Spike strips were effective, but they could escalate situations quite quickly,” Dekops said.

“This approach gives drivers a chance to reflect, reset, and make a better decision.”

The LED strips activate during pursuits, forming a glowing lane of motivational messaging designed to gently encourage deceleration and voluntary stopping.
In early trials, one driver reportedly slowed significantly after encountering repeated messages reading “You Are Enough” across the road surface.

However, in another case, a vehicle continued through the illuminated strip while it updated to:

“We Still Believe In You — Please Consider Stopping.”
Officers say the system has changed the dynamic of pursuits.

“It feels less like forcing an outcome and more like guiding one,” one officer said.

Public reaction has been mixed.\

“Yeah nah, I reckon tyres going flat worked quicker,” one motorist said.

Another added,

“Bit of a confidence boost before getting pulled over though.”

Police confirmed traditional spike strips are still carried in some vehicles but are now classified as “legacy tools”, requiring additional approval before use.

“This is about safer roads and better interactions,” Dekops said.

As of publication, the most effective message appears to be:

“Stop — You Are Enough (But So Is Everyone Else On The Road).” See less
— in West Coast, New Zealand.

Another un-ai'ed bit.  An honest journal he said.

Well I choose to hear that I suppose.

We spoke about that feeling that when you were young, everyone else is on the fairground ride having a ball it seems but you are pulled off it early doors,  and get to see all the rest.  It's bullshit really - I often feel (when I reflect on reflections like that) like these are fictions of the mind to explain feelings in the present.

It degrades their value, because it feeds the notion, I am at best disingenuous, at worst a fiction maker of convenience. It's balm of sorts I suppose, or is it merely my attempt at piffy-eiffy justification for doing what I know is not right.

It hurts,  all the friends I have lost and all the time I have been in these many many tunnels of thoughts that sprawl all over the place and make navigation and meaningful sense so elusive.

What am I recording today?  We have decided to sell the house - well appointed an agent that will cost a bloody fortune if we don't.  I am truly mixed - the collateral damage of last year is all over this place I thought I would never want to leave but if feels too hard to stay.

I've bleed my dreams on to these streets and now the rain has washed away those hopes.  Left a permanent stench of failure and I am left fighting the battle of the ages - shame vs guilt,  I did vs I am.  Answer as ever is complicated and most certainly a combo of course.

That's enough positivity for one entry!

essays.body:
Arrived late yesterday, well later than we had planned,  but no drama.  It's a beautiful spot and we have been exceptionally lucky to find it.  

We both need to relax more than ever.  We have many difficult decisions ahead,  and their proximity will make them harder still.  So no more on that for now.

This place is super-private,  and has a spectacular view.  I stood in my birthday-suit this morning looking out at the bay.  It's spectacular and so very quite,  no sign of others anywhere. A very reasonable expectation of privacy, hence the special suit.  Their are some distant properties ( if they have binoculars they are welcome to the show ).    Mountainous green vegetation of different classes and shades meet an out of sight flat sandy beach and blend to the backdrop of glorious blues of lite and deep depth water across the expansive bay with large and small satellites of green on their unblenished small sandy shores.   

Feeling the gently rays of sun and light wind across my wholly exposed self and gazing upon that picture of perfect and serene nature makes me feel this is exactly what I need right now.

essays.title: Feedback from AI - Day 1 entry
essays.body:
## Assessment

This is a **strong first journal entry** because it does three useful things:

1. **It establishes place** — private, beautiful, remote, restorative.
2. **It establishes emotional context** — you are carrying difficult decisions but deliberately choosing not to let them dominate the entry.
3. **It has a distinctive human voice** — the “birthday-suit” line gives it warmth, humour, and specificity.

The best part is the final emotional turn:

> “...makes me feel this is exactly what I need right now.”

That gives the entry purpose. It is not just a travel description; it is a record of *why this place matters at this moment*.

## What weakens it

The main issue is that the richest descriptive sentence becomes overloaded:

> “Mountainous green vegetation of different classes and shades meet an out of sight flat sandy beach and blend to the backdrop…”

There are lovely images in there, but too many are competing at once. The sentence tries to describe hills, vegetation, beach, water, islands, colour, distance, and mood all in one breath. That makes the beauty slightly harder to feel.

There are also a few small technical fixes:

| Original                | Suggested                                                          |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **quite**               | **quiet**                                                          |
| **Their are**           | **There are**                                                      |
| **lite**                | **light**                                                          |
| **gently rays**         | **gentle rays**                                                    |
| **unblenished**         | **unblemished**                                                    |
| **wholly exposed self** | maybe **bare skin**, **whole exposed body**, or **uncovered self** |

The phrase **“birthday-suit”** works because it breaks the seriousness and gives the entry personality. I would keep it, but tighten the surrounding wording so the joke lands cleanly and does not become over-explained.

## Improved version — polished but still your voice

> Arrived late yesterday — later than planned — but with no drama. It is a beautiful spot, and we have been exceptionally lucky to find it.
>
> We both need to relax more than ever. There are difficult decisions ahead of us, and the closeness of them makes them harder still. So no more on that for now.
>
> This place is wonderfully private, with a spectacular view over the bay. I stood in my birthday suit this morning, looking out across it. No sign of anyone nearby. A very reasonable expectation of privacy, hence the special suit. There are a few distant properties, but if anyone has binoculars, they are welcome to the show.
>
> The hills are thick with green vegetation, layered in different shades and textures, falling away toward a hidden sandy beach. Beyond it, the bay opens into bands of blue — pale light near the shore, deeper water further out — with small green islands scattered across it, each edged with untouched strips of sand.
>
> Feeling the gentle sun and light wind across my bare skin, while looking out at that calm, perfect sweep of nature, I felt something settle in me. This is exactly what I need right now.

## Slightly more literary version

> We arrived late yesterday, later than planned, but without drama. It is a beautiful spot, and we have been absurdly lucky to find it.
>
> We both need to relax more than ever. There are difficult decisions waiting for us, and their nearness makes them heavier. But not today. No more on that for now.
>
> The house is deeply private, with a view that feels almost indecently generous. This morning I stood in my birthday suit looking out over the bay. There was no sign of anyone, no movement from any nearby place, only the quiet and the view. A reasonable expectation of privacy, I decided. Hence the special suit. There are a few distant houses, but if they have binoculars, they are welcome to the show.
>
> Green hills drop toward a hidden strip of pale sand. The vegetation changes shade as it falls — dark, bright, silvered, dense — before giving way to the blues of the bay. Near the shore the water is light and glassy; further out it deepens. Small green islands sit across it like quiet satellites, each with its own clean edge of sand.
>
> The sun was gentle on my skin, the wind light, the world briefly asking nothing of me. Standing there, wholly exposed and oddly safe, I felt the truth of it: this is exactly what I need right now.

## Best improvement principle

For this style of journal writing, your strongest move is:

**Keep the emotional honesty, but simplify the visual sentences.**

The writing works best when it alternates between:

* plain emotional truth
* one clear sensory image
* a small human aside
* another clear image
* a final reflective sentence

That rhythm suits this piece well.

essays.title: Introduction
essays.body:
I have had depression all of my adult life.  In my experience, people find comfort in feeling they know what ails them.  In my case,  and in my line of work it can seem like a badge,  as in an ID, a credential.  I've spent the best part of 15 years in this line of work, and unless you or someone you love has needed my type of services, it's unlikely you've heard of my trade.  

I am Peer Support Worker, it doesn't sound grand does it?  Nothing much to write home about.  Not exactly - look ma - I made it,  I'm a doctor, a neurosurgeon - I did my time and training and now I save lives before breakfast, most days.  No, there is not really any universal claim to fame, and certainly none to fortune, in my line of work.    

Why then do I bother to put pen to paper.  Well, put simple,  any decent neurosurgeon would cry out for the help I can provide if he or she or someone they love felt the needed it.  In exactly the same way,  I or you would cry out for a neurosurgeon when and if misfortune created the need in us or our loved ones.

This is a memoir of sorts, a tale of how I have chosen, in-part, to devote the energy and enthusiasm, such as my trauma and illness allows me to possess, to a group who have had similar experiences and struggles to my own.

Much more importantly, it's an attempt to explain a movement that I belief has already done immeasurable good for many - both those who have practiced it and those that have found themselves in need.  That said,  it is woefully misunderstood and the


and as such I'lTl come on to explain why I think that statement true and why the value of peer support remains untapped.

essays.title: History
essays.body:
Peer support, in its modern form, is not a single thing. It is a layer cake of aspiration and need, born from an acute shortage of understanding, an absence of humane care, and an abundance of misunderstanding and fear.

Its genealogy stretches back more than a century, to unclaimed beginnings in mutual aid: people, often excluded from formal care and sometimes from society itself, forming fragile networks of support because there was nowhere else to turn. These early efforts were not always named, funded, professionalised, or recognised as care at all. They were practical before they were theoretical. One person who had survived something recognised something in another person, and that recognition changed what became possible.

That absence matters. It was not an abstract gap in provision, but the ordinary and brutal fact of people having no useful language offered to them, no safe place to go, and no care that did not also carry fear. Peer support first grew in that gap. It emerged where systems failed, where families were overwhelmed, where institutions isolated people, and where those experiencing distress had to find one another in order to remain human in their own eyes.

It is tempting to tell this history as a practical answer to shortage: fewer beds, fewer workers, more need, and peer support appearing as the layer that fills the missing space. There is truth in that, but it is not the whole truth. The counter-case is just as important. Once mutual aid is brought inside institutions, it can stop being unclaimed. It can become supervised, measured, professionalised, and translated back into the language of the very systems it first answered. The cost is not only political. It is felt in the room: in what can be said, what has to be recorded, what must be softened, and what must be made safe for the service rather than for the person seeking support.

Peer support, then, can be understood as a layered response to absence: an accumulation of need, protest, care, and aspiration. It is not a cleanly defined movement. Each layer formed in reaction to what was missing at the time: first the raw mutual aid of people left to care for one another in the absence of formal systems; then the post-war emergence of self-organised institutions; then the more explicit language of survivor-led, consumer-led, and lived-experience practice. Each layer carries the mark of the one beneath it. Even when the language becomes more formal, the originating pressure remains the same: people left to make sense with one another because other forms of care had failed them, had harmed them, or had not arrived.

The founding of Fountain House sits squarely within this lineage. It emerged not from theory first, but from a practical lack of understanding, care, and meaningful support for people living with mental distress. Before it became a model, it answered a need: the need for somewhere to be, something to do, and someone who did not begin from misunderstanding.

It is within this context that the clubhouse model, exemplified by Fountain House, introduced a quietly radical proposition: that community is therapy. This was not simply a philosophical stance. It was a direct response to the fear and misunderstanding surrounding mental illness. Where traditional systems isolated, pathologised, and controlled, the clubhouse model sought to integrate, dignify, and involve. Members were not patients but participants.

That change in wording is not cosmetic. To be called a member rather than a patient alters the terms on which a person enters the room. It shifts attention from what is wrong with them to what they can share, hold, make, repeat, and return to. The environment itself — shared work, shared responsibility, shared presence — becomes the medium through which recovery is supported. In this way, the model addresses not only clinical gaps but social ones, restoring connection where there has been rupture.

If the American lineage gave peer support some of its early structure, the UK and Europe gave it friction, critique, and, in many ways, its political voice. There too, the movement formed in the same absence: of understanding, of humane care, and of respect for the knowledge of those who had lived through distress. But it developed in closer dialogue with state systems, and often in direct opposition to them.

That opposition was not an added theory placed on top of experience. It came from being named, treated, managed, and spoken for. It came from the slow insistence that those experiences generated knowledge rather than disqualifying it.

In the United Kingdom, the late twentieth century saw the rise of organised survivor movements that rejected the dominant medical framing of mental illness as the only legitimate account. Groups such as the Mental Patients’ Union in the 1970s articulated, with unusual clarity, that those receiving care were not passive recipients but individuals with rights, agency, and insight into their own experiences. This was not simply peer support as mutual aid. It was peer support as resistance.

The resistance sits in the refusal of passivity: not only receiving care, but questioning the terms of that care; not only being described, but answering back with a description of one’s own.

By the 1980s and 1990s, networks such as the Hearing Voices Network reframed experiences that had long been pathologised. Hearing voices was no longer treated solely as a symptom to be eliminated, but as an experience that could be explored, understood, and lived with. This shift did not deny distress. Rather, it challenged the idea that distress exhausted the meaning of the experience. People were invited to speak from within their experience, not merely be spoken about from outside it.

Across Europe, similar developments took shape in different forms, shaped by local health systems, welfare states, activist traditions, and psychiatric histories. The common thread was the claim that lived experience mattered not only as testimony, but as knowledge. Peer support in this context was not merely kindness between people with similar histories. It was also a challenge to who gets to define suffering, recovery, risk, capacity, and care.

This is one of the great tensions in the history of peer support. Its moral force comes from mutuality, recognition, and shared humanity. Its political force comes from the same place, but under pressure: the refusal to be reduced to a case, a diagnosis, a problem, or an object of professional management. The peer is not powerful because they know everything. The peer is powerful because they know something from the inside that cannot be fully substituted by policy, training, or clinical distance.

Beyond North America and Europe, peer support has followed no single path. In some places it has been shaped by community health movements, in others by human rights work, disability activism, post-institutional reform, or the practical need to extend care where formal services are thin. The danger in describing this global development is that the phrase “global peer support movement” can make the history sound smoother and more unified than it is. It is better understood as a family of related responses to different absences.

In low-resource settings, peer-led and community-based approaches often carry particular promise because formal mental health systems may be limited, distant, or overburdened. But the promise should not be overstated. Evidence that peer-led recovery groups are acceptable or promising is not the same as proof that they can be scaled without care, resourced properly without distortion, or protected from becoming a cheap substitute for services that should exist. “Promising” points to an opening, not a conclusion.

In Australia and New Zealand, peer support took shape within publicly funded health systems that were, at once, expanding and under strain. Here, the movement developed less as open resistance and more as gradual, often hard-won integration, though it carried the same underlying insistence: that lived experience is not an adjunct to care, but a form of expertise in its own right.

The phrase “hard-won” matters because integration can look smooth from a policy distance. Up close, it means negotiating the terms on which lived experience is allowed into the room, and what it is asked to leave outside in order to be accepted.

From the late twentieth century onward, both Australia and New Zealand saw increasing recognition of peer support as a legitimate and necessary component of mental health services. In Australia, advocacy bodies and consumer-led movements helped formalise the role of consumers and carers in shaping policy and service delivery. Peer workers began to be employed within clinical teams, not merely as symbolic inclusions, but as contributors whose insights could alter the nature of care itself.

That alteration is the stake: whether lived experience is invited in to confirm an existing system, or whether it is permitted to disturb the assumptions of that system.

In New Zealand, this integration carried an additional and essential dimension: the influence of Māori models of health and wellbeing. Frameworks such as Te Whare Tapa Whā emphasise a holistic understanding of wellbeing, one that includes not only mental health, but physical, spiritual, family, and communal dimensions. This perspective aligns naturally with peer support principles because it resists the reduction of recovery to symptom management alone.

It also places pressure on the word “recovery” itself. Recovery must hold more than clinical improvement. It must be able to hold whānau, spirit, body, connection, culture, belonging, and the conditions that make balance possible.

Organisations such as Te Pou have played an important role in developing the peer workforce in Aotearoa New Zealand, providing training, guidance, and a growing evidence base for the value of lived-experience roles. Over time, peer support in Aotearoa became both embedded within services and distinct from them, maintaining its ethos of mutuality and authenticity even as it entered more formal structures.

That “both” is not easy. Embeddedness can bring reach, funding, protection, and legitimacy. Distinctness protects the very thing that made peer support necessary in the first place.

What characterises the Australia–New Zealand strand is this careful balancing act. Integration brings legitimacy, funding, and reach, but it also carries the risk of dilution: peer support becoming absorbed into the very systems it once stood apart from. The ongoing work, then, is not simply expansion, but preservation. It is the work of holding onto mutuality, shared experience, and human connection while operating within institutional frameworks.

The consequence of losing that balance would be concrete: peer workers present in services but unable to practise mutuality; lived experience named in policy but thinned into a role description; connection spoken of, but supervised into something safer for the institution than for the person seeking support.

At its best, this regional development demonstrates something quietly powerful. Peer support does not need to remain at the margins to retain its integrity. It can exist within systems and still challenge them, provided its foundations remain intact. The movement continues its layered evolution, adapting to context but anchored in the same enduring truth: people who have lived through distress have something essential to offer one another.

That truth endures because it is practical before it is theoretical. One person recognises something in another, and that recognition changes what becomes possible.

What makes this history coherent, despite its layered and sometimes fragmented development, is the continuity of its underlying impulse. From mutual aid to structured community, from survival to self-determination, each layer responds to the same core deficit: the absence of humane, understanding support.

The clubhouse model does not replace these earlier forms but builds upon them, offering a more organised expression of the same principle. It meets practical needs — housing, work, routine — but also honours the deeper human requirements for belonging, recognition, and purpose. Those practical needs should stay practical on the page: a place to live, a reason to get up, a repeated task, another person expecting you to return. Without those, belonging remains only a word.

In that sense, peer support is not just a service or an intervention. It is an ongoing act of reclamation. The clubhouse model stands as one of its more visible forms, but it remains part of a broader, living tradition: one that continues to evolve wherever systems do not understand enough, wherever care is too thin, and wherever people still have to find one another.

From a personal perspective, peer support had no real context or meaning to me until I was visited by a man about ten years my senior. Before that visit, the word sat at a distance, more like a role or policy term than a human encounter. What changed was not a definition first, but the presence of someone older, near enough in experience to make the idea intelligible, standing inside a space that had previously been only language.

That is perhaps the smallest and clearest version of the whole history. Before peer support is a workforce, a model, a policy category, or an evidence base, it is this: one person who has been somewhere difficult sitting with another person who is there now, and making it just a little more possible to be.

essays.title: Julie
essays.body:
Julie was born into what, from the outside, might have passed as a functional family in 1950s Waikato, New Zealand. Inside, things were more complicated. Her father drank, her mother controlled, yet in those early years there was still something that felt, at times, like safety. For a while, she was simply a child—content, developing as expected, unaware of the deeper currents shaping the ground beneath her.

Ada endured. She raised eight children in a corrugated iron cottage, where survival depended on endurance and ingenuity—especially the quiet art of keeping money, and hope, out of John’s reach when drink took hold. The cottage had to hold all of them: the children, the labour, the silence after he returned, the small calculations that kept the next day possible. She would know what could be spent before he asked, what could be hidden before he looked, what word had to stay behind her teeth. It was not only money she learned to hide. It was expectation. A coin put aside, a word not spoken, a face held still until the danger passed. Her hands did the work and then gave nothing away. The children learned the shape of that silence too, how a room could narrow around a footstep, how tomorrow might depend on a coin no one admitted was there.

Their son George, Julie’s grandfather, was small and physically fragile. He survived the mines, only to have his lungs ravaged by gas in the trenches of the Great War. He came home alive, but altered—dependent on brandy to steady what remained of him. He married Mary, a local woman determined enough to believe she might save him. They settled on a small dairy block near Matamata. George was not violent, but he was absent in his own way—disappearing for hours into the cowshed with his flask, leaving Mary to carry both the farm and their son. The cowshed became the place where he could vanish while still being close enough to be counted as present. Mary would have known the sound of that absence: work continuing, a child waiting, the flask somewhere out of sight but not out of mind.

That son, Jim—Julie’s father—was born in 1928. He grew up watching his mother do everything while his father faded. Little survives of his early years, but like many of his generation, hardship arrived young and stayed. Still barely a man, he was drawn into the next war. Like the Hewitt men before him, he survived through resilience, humour, and alcohol. Survival had a shape in that family. It looked like carrying on, saying little, making light, and reaching for drink when silence was no longer enough.

In later life, Jim could be charming—the joker at the pub, the entertainer. At home, he was something else: volatile, haunted, unpredictable. The same humour that drew people toward him could disappear at the door. A room might hold itself differently when he entered; voices adjusting, bodies waiting to see which version had come home. He married Julie’s mother, Eileen, drawn to something he had never known—a sense of steadiness, of hope, of goodness that seemed, for a moment, within reach.

Eileen came from a different lineage. The Ealders were a well-regarded family of Scottish border stock who settled in Te Awamutu. Their legacy rested on a rigid belief: that appearance and virtue were one and the same. Eileen, born in 1933, embodied that ideal. She was a star pupil, a prefect, eventually head girl—someone who learned early that perfection was not optional but expected. Her own mother enforced that standard without compromise. To be seen doing well was not separate from being good. A mistake was not just a mistake; it was something that showed.

She met Jim on one of his better days. Without the language—or permission—to understand what drew her to him, she convinced herself she saw something redeemable. She believed that with enough structure, enough order, enough control, she could contain his drinking and tidy the chaos. When that belief proved false, the control did not disappear—it turned inward, then outward again, focused almost entirely on her only child. What could not be contained in him had to be contained somewhere. Julie became the place where order could still be demanded.

By the time Julie was born, on a bright day in Hamilton in 1954, these two histories had closed in around her. From her father’s side came instability: a house thick with the smell of stale alcohol, where tension could turn without warning into anger or violence. From her mother’s side came the response: tightening control, rigid expectations, the constant pressure to be right, to be perfect, to compensate for what could not be fixed. Before Julie could understand any of it, her body would have learned the signs: the change in a voice, the pause before a reply, the need to become smaller without being told.

Those early lessons did not arrive as thoughts she could name. They settled instead as feelings—quiet, persistent, difficult to place. A sense, at first vague, that something about her did not sit quite right in the world she had been given. Not wrong in a way she could explain. More like being expected to stand in a place that was almost, but not quite, hers.

As a young child, Julie did not think in terms of identity or difference. She noticed things. She watched boys and felt something closer to recognition than curiosity. The expectations placed on her—small, domestic, contained—felt less like guidance and more like constraint. None of it came as a single moment. It gathered slowly, piece by piece, forming a question she did not yet have the language to ask or the self-awareness to acknowledge. She could not have said what she wanted. She only knew, in certain moments, that what was being offered to her did not fit in her hands.

At school, the lines were clearer. Boys on one side, girls on the other—games, uniforms, behaviour, futures implied in the smallest routines. Julie learned where she was expected to stand, how she was meant to behave, what was required to avoid attention. She also learned, without ever being told directly, that stepping outside those lines carried a cost, the inflation age would place on it was not yet grasped as her young mind reasoned compliance the lesser evil. So she watched first. She let her eyes find the place she was meant to go, then put her body there. Each small act of compliance bought quiet, and took something with it.

At home, there was no space for any kind of uncertainty. Her mother valued order, correctness, presentation. Her father’s volatility left little room for anything that might provoke acknowledgement of her existing, let alone any particular aspect thereof.  Confusion or challenge. So Julie did what children do when there is no safe place to test a feeling: she kept it to herself. Keeping it meant listening before speaking. It meant measuring the room. It meant letting a thought pass through her and then closing around it before anyone else could see.

Still, the sense did not leave. It sharpened in quiet moments—when she caught her reflection and felt a distance from it, when she imagined herself moving through the world differently, when the roles laid out before her felt not just unwanted but misaligned. It was not yet a declaration, not even a fully formed thought. It was a tension, constant and low, like a note held just out of tune. She might look away from the reflection before she had finished seeing it, not because it answered anything, but because it asked too much.

She did not yet think, *I am the wrong gender*. That clarity would come much later. What she knew, in the beginning, was simpler and more unsettling: that the person others seemed to see was not the one she felt herself to be. The difference lived under ordinary things: where she stood, what she wore, how she was spoken to, what future was quietly being arranged around her.

And so, alongside everything else she was learning—how to read a room, how to anticipate moods, how to stay within the narrow edges of safety—Julie began learning something quieter. How to carry a private truth without words.  The more telling tale of her point of difference was she related more to her father than to her mother.  Not to his drinking, nor to the danger in him, but to the place he occupied in the family’s imagination: male, unknowable, given a kind of distance no one seemed to question. Her mother’s world of correctness and presentation offered no shelter for what Julie could not yet say.

She grew up between those forces—her father’s unpredictability and her mother’s discipline—learning that safety was conditional, and peace was fragile. Peace meant no sudden turn in the room. Safety meant nothing had been noticed.

She was the third generation in a family where the men disappeared into the bottle, and the women survived by containing what could not be escaped.

essays.title: Too much too soon but not enough
essays.body:
## The Full Story Arc. 

### The World.

St. Cormac's College, somewhere in the English Home Counties, 1986. Ivy-choked red brick, cold dormitories, the smell of floor polish and incense. A school that takes boys at thirteen and returns them at eighteen as lawyers, bankers, and Members of Parliament — or breaks them quietly in the process, with nobody outside the walls ever knowing which.

The institution runs on hierarchy, silence, and the unspoken compact that what happens here stays here. Masters wear black gowns. The chapel bell marks every hour. Beatings are administered with a cane kept on a hook behind the headmaster's door and logged in a ledger as though they were library fines. The soccer pitch is the one place a boy can breathe — and even there, the wrong kind of victory earns the wrong kind of attention.

It is a world built to produce men. It has no vocabulary for boys like Jake and Marcus.

---

### The Boys Arrive

**Jake Hartley** comes from old money and a father who played for the school in 1962 and has the photograph on his study wall. He arrives at St. Cormac's trailing expectation like a coat too large for him. He grows into it quickly. By the third year he is exactly what the school wants — gifted, charismatic, unbothered by the cold and the discipline in the way that only boys who've never had to be afraid can be unbothered.

**Marcus Webb** arrives on a partial scholarship, which everyone knows and nobody says. His mother, Diana Webb, is the kind of woman who compensates for insecurity with ferocity. She is beautiful, socially ambitious, and absolutely certain about everything. She has decided Marcus will be a credit to her, will reflect her upward, and she attends every parents' day in clothes slightly too expensive for the occasion. She does not ask Marcus how he is. She asks him what he's achieved.

Marcus learns early that the gap between who he is and who his mother requires him to be is not a problem to be solved. It is simply the condition of his life.

---

### Brother Declan

Every such school has one. Brother Declan teaches Latin and runs the junior dormitory. He is charming in the way that specific kind of dangerous man is always charming — attentive, conspiratorial, good at making a boy feel chosen. He has been at St. Cormac's for eleven years. There are boys who've left and said nothing. There are boys still there, saying nothing. The silence is load-bearing. The institution rests on it.

He has favourites. Everyone knows this. What everyone knows and nobody says is what being a favourite means.

---

### The Third Boy — Thomas

Thomas Ellery is not one of the protagonists. He is something worse: a supporting character, which means the story can spend him.

Thomas is slight, gentle, academically brilliant, with a laugh that makes a room warmer. He is also transparently, helplessly himself in a place that punishes exactly that. He doesn't have Marcus's armour or Jake's social capital. He attaches to both of them — drawn to Marcus because Marcus is quietly kind to him, drawn to Jake because Jake once told a prefect to leave him alone and meant it.

Brother Declan notices Thomas in the second year.

What follows is told in fragments throughout the story — a detail here, a silence there, the way Thomas stops meeting people's eyes, the way he flinches in Latin class. Marcus sees it first because Marcus watches everything. He tries, carefully, to be present for Thomas without naming what he suspects, because naming it would require a conversation neither of them has the language for and which could go terribly wrong in a school like this.

Jake doesn't see it, not until much later, and his not-seeing becomes one of the fractures between them.

---

### Diana Webb — The Worst of Them

She arrives at the story through a parents' evening in the spring term of the fourth year.

She has found something in Marcus's room during the Christmas holidays. Not evidence of anything acted upon — just a notebook, a few pages, the kind of private half-articulated thing a lonely boy writes at fifteen when he's trying to understand himself. She reads it. She does not speak to Marcus about it. She speaks to the school.

What makes Diana Webb the true villain of this story — worse than Brother Declan, in a specific way, because Declan is a predator acting on appetite while Diana acts on *love twisted beyond recognition* — is that she genuinely believes she is saving her son. Her horror at what she's read is not performance. She really does believe homosexuality is a sickness, a sin, a social death sentence. She really does believe that the worst thing that could happen to Marcus is to be what he is.

She meets privately with Brother Declan. This is the nauseating irony at the heart of the story — the one person in the institution who has most damaged boys like Marcus is the person she trusts to *fix* her son. Declan is smooth and reassuring. He suggests the friendship with Jake is an unhealthy attachment and that Marcus would benefit from closer pastoral supervision.

He volunteers for it himself.

---

### The Fracture Lines

Marcus doesn't know what his mother has done. He only notices that Brother Declan is suddenly interested in him, and that interest fills him with a cold, specific dread he can't explain to anyone.

He pulls back from Jake. Not entirely — they still train together, still talk — but there is a new guardedness, a door slightly closed that was open before. Jake feels it like a change in weather without understanding the cause. He compensates the way golden boys compensate: by being more, by being louder, by dating a girl from the village whose name he'll barely remember in a year.

Thomas, watching all of this from the periphery, understands more than either of them.

---

### The Night It Breaks

A Tuesday in February. Sleet on the windows. Thomas has been called to Brother Declan's study three times that week for what the ledger records as "additional Latin tuition."

Marcus finds him afterwards, in the bathroom at the end of the dormitory corridor, sitting on the cold tile floor with his back against the wall. Marcus sits down next to him without a word and they stay there for a long time. Thomas says, very quietly, "I can't do this anymore." Marcus doesn't fully understand the scope of what he means. He thinks he means the school, the cold, the grinding relentlessness of it. He says, "I know. But you can. You're nearly through the year."

Thomas nods. He seems calmer when Marcus leaves.

The next morning his bed is empty.

---

### The Aftermath

The school's response is a masterclass in institutional self-protection. A private funeral. A letter to parents emphasising the pastoral care available to boys who are struggling. Thomas's name is not read at chapel. Within a fortnight the official position is grief, silence, and moving on.

Brother Declan gives a reading at the memorial service.

What happens next is where Diana Webb becomes unforgivable.

She has been told — by Declan, to protect himself, to redirect — that Marcus and Thomas had an *unhealthy relationship.* That Marcus's *influence* was a factor. She doesn't need much. She has been looking for someone to be responsible for what her son is, and here is a narrative handed to her. She begins, with the particular skill of a certain kind of intelligent, frightened parent, to work it. A word to Thomas's mother. A word to Jake's father.

Jake hears it third-hand, filtered through grief and shock and a fifteen-year-old's limited ability to interrogate a story told by an adult with authority. The version that reaches him is not the truth. It is the version that makes Marcus culpable, that makes the closeness between Marcus and Thomas something predatory rather than protective. 

Jake doesn't believe it — not exactly. But he doesn't *not* believe it. And Marcus, when he tries to explain, finds that grief has made him inarticulate and that Jake's eyes have changed in a way he doesn't know how to reach past.

---

### The Separation

Marcus is moved. Diana Webb requests it, in writing, citing her son's "difficult associations" and "the pastoral concerns raised by the school." St. Cormac's is relieved to have a clean solution to a complicated situation.

He is transferred mid-year to Alderton College. The school across the valley. The rival school. The one St. Cormac's has beaten in the county cup four years running and intends to beat again.

Jake watches him go. They don't say a real goodbye. Diana Webb makes sure of that.

---

### The Separate Years

At Alderton, Marcus rebuilds slowly. The school is less gothic, less cruel — not kind, exactly, but less actively hostile to the fact of him. He finds a different kind of space to breathe. He makes the first team by autumn. He does not make close friends. He writes letters to Jake that he doesn't send. He thinks about Thomas every day.

At St. Cormac's, Jake has the year everyone expects him to have — better than ever on the pitch, predicted top grades, girls, parties, the full performance of being Jake Hartley. He is miserable in a way he has no framework for. He picks fights. He is short with people who love him. He lies awake at night replaying the conversation where he didn't say the right thing to Marcus and trying to identify the exact moment he could have said it.

Brother Declan is eventually dismissed — quietly, a "mutual decision," with a reference that says nothing incriminating. He goes to another school. This is not a redemption story.

---

### The Cup Final

May. A neutral pitch, halfway between both schools. Thick spring mud. The kind of grey English afternoon that feels like it exists outside of time.

Both teams know who they're playing. The boys from St. Cormac's have been winding each other up about Alderton for weeks — the defector, the boy who went to the other side. Jake's teammates say things to him about Marcus that they think are funny. Jake doesn't respond. He laces his boots and walks out.

They see each other during warm-up. Across the pitch, through the grey air. 

Neither of them waves.

The game is brutal in the way that cup finals between genuine rivals always are — everything underneath the surface finally given permission to come out. Jake is extraordinary, which he usually is. Marcus matches him, which he didn't always used to be able to. They spend the match in each other's orbit, as they always have — drawn together and pulling apart, reading each other's movement before it happens, tackling each other with more force than necessary and with something that is not quite anger.

It goes to extra time. Then penalties. Then, somehow, to a moment that isn't in any rulebook — the final penalty taken, scored, the referee's whistle, and two boys standing in the mud twenty metres apart with the game between them finally, suddenly, over.

Marcus walks toward Jake. Or Jake walks toward Marcus. Later, neither will be certain who moved first.

What happens is not planned and not performed. It is just two boys who have been separated by grief and manipulation and a year of distance, standing close enough to see each other clearly for the first time since February, and all of the careful management of feeling simply running out.

They hold on too long. And then — in the mud, in front of everyone, on a school football pitch in England in 1986 — they kiss.

---

### The Ripping Apart

It lasts perhaps ten seconds.

Then the hands come — fathers, mostly, and a couple of coaches — and the shouting, and the pulling, and Marcus and Jake are separated with the particular violence that frightened people bring to the thing they're frightened of. The crowd on the touchline is a wall of coats and red faces. Someone is screaming. Someone else is laughing.

They are dragged in opposite directions.

The last thing they see is each other — Jake twisting back, Marcus being marched forward, both of them still catching their breath.

---

### The Ending

The story ends there, unresolved, the way real things often are. No reconciliation yet. No understanding from the world around them. Just two boys who loved each other in a world that had no place for it — and the memory of ten seconds in the mud at the end of a cup final, which nobody and nothing can take back, however hard they try.

Somewhere in it is Thomas. And the notebook Diana Webb read. And the specific, irreversible weight of what happens when adults handle fragile things as though they are weapons.

The last line is Chuck's line, transposed:

*They smashed it. But it wasn't the way they said.*

essays.title: Too much too soon but not enough
essays.body:
The Full Story Arc (draft 2 Revised)

The World

St. Cormac’s College, somewhere in the English Home Counties, 1986. Ivy-choked red brick, cold dormitories, the smell of floor polish and incense. A school that takes boys at thirteen and returns them at eighteen as lawyers, bankers, and Members of Parliament — or breaks them quietly in the process, with nobody outside the walls ever knowing which.

The institution runs on hierarchy, silence, and the unspoken compact that what happens here stays here. Masters wear black gowns. The chapel bell marks every hour. Beatings are administered with a cane kept on a hook behind the headmaster’s door and logged in a ledger as though they were library fines. The soccer pitch is the one place a boy can breathe — and even there, the wrong kind of victory earns the wrong kind of attention.

It is a world built to produce men. It has no vocabulary for boys like Jake and Marcus.


---

The Boys Arrive

Jake Hartley comes from old money and a father who played for the school in 1962 and has the photograph on his study wall. He arrives at St. Cormac’s trailing expectation like a coat too large for him. He grows into it quickly. By the third year he is exactly what the school wants — gifted, charismatic, unbothered by the cold and the discipline in the way that only boys who have never had to be afraid can be unbothered.

But there are moments that don’t fit. He chooses, once, to stand with Marcus instead of laughing with a prefect, and pays for it with a week of colder treatment from boys whose approval he usually commands. He doesn’t mention it. He doesn’t need to. Marcus notices.

Jake talks easily about everything except the things that matter. When those surface, he circles them, impatient, as though language has failed him personally.


---

Marcus Webb arrives on a partial scholarship, which everyone knows and nobody says. His mother, Diana Webb, is the kind of woman who compensates for insecurity with certainty. She is beautiful, socially ambitious, and absolutely convinced of her own correctness. She attends every parents’ day in clothes slightly too expensive for the occasion. She does not ask Marcus how he is. She asks him what he’s achieved.

Once, before a term begins, she straightens his tie in the car and tells him she is proud of him. It is the only time she says it without qualification. Marcus carries it for years.

He learns early that the gap between who he is and who his mother requires him to be is not a problem to be solved. It is simply the condition of his life.


---

Brother Declan

Every such school has one. Brother Declan teaches Latin and runs the junior dormitory. He is attentive, precise, remembers small details about boys — a translation corrected gently, a name remembered, a quiet word after class. He is trusted.

He has been at St. Cormac’s for eleven years. There are boys who have left and said nothing. There are boys still there, saying nothing. The silence is load-bearing.

He has favourites. Everyone knows this. What everyone knows and nobody says is what being a favourite means.


---

The Third Boy — Thomas

Thomas Ellery is not one of the protagonists. He is something worse: a supporting character, which means the story can spend him.

He is slight, gentle, academically brilliant, with a laugh that arrives unexpectedly and makes a room warmer. Once, in the dormitory, he explains a line of Latin poetry with such quiet enthusiasm that even Jake listens, grinning, though he understands none of it. For a moment, the place feels almost human.

Thomas attaches to both of them — drawn to Marcus because Marcus is quietly kind, drawn to Jake because Jake once told a prefect to leave him alone and meant it.

Jake, off-balance one evening, finds himself talking to Thomas in a way he doesn’t with anyone else. Not a confession. Nothing so clear. But he talks about Marcus — about the way Marcus thinks, the way he notices things, the way being around him feels different and he doesn’t know why. He becomes irritated with himself halfway through, as though the words are failing to land correctly.

Thomas understands before Jake does. He says nothing that would force it into the open. He lets Jake have the safety of not knowing.

Brother Declan notices Thomas in the second year.


---

The Fracture Begins

What follows is told in fragments — a detail here, a silence there. Thomas stops meeting people’s eyes. He flinches once in Latin class and covers it with a laugh that doesn’t arrive fully.

Marcus sees it first because Marcus watches everything. He considers saying something — to a master, to Jake — and does not. There is no language for what he suspects, and in a place like this, being wrong would be dangerous.

Jake notices something, once. A hesitation, a look. He dismisses it. There is always something wrong with someone in a place like this. He has learned not to dwell.

Thomas carries what he knows — about himself, about Marcus, about Jake — and what is being done to him, and does not share any of it in a way that could be heard.


---

Diana Webb — The Curator

During the Christmas holidays of the fourth year, Diana finds a notebook in Marcus’s room. It contains nothing explicit — just fragments, questions, the half-articulated attempts of a boy trying to understand himself.

She reads it.

She does not speak to Marcus about it.

She goes to the school.

She meets privately with Brother Declan. He listens, attentive, reassuring. He suggests that Marcus may be forming unhealthy attachments, that certain friendships can become intense in ways that are not helpful. He does not name anything directly. He does not need to.

Diana does not invent a story. She selects one.

To the school, she speaks of pastoral concerns.
To Jake’s father, she expresses quiet unease about Marcus’s influence.
To Thomas’s family, later, she allows the suggestion of intensity, dependency, something not quite right.

Each version is plausible. Together, they distort everything.

She believes she is saving her son.

Declan volunteers to take a closer pastoral interest in Marcus.


---

The Night It Breaks

A Tuesday in February. Sleet on the windows.

Thomas has been called to Brother Declan’s study three times that week for “additional Latin tuition.”

Marcus finds him afterwards, in the bathroom at the end of the dormitory corridor, sitting on the cold tile floor with his back against the wall.

Marcus sits down next to him without a word.

After a long time, Thomas says, very quietly, “It doesn’t stop.”

Marcus hears something else. The school. The pressure. The endlessness of it.

He says, “I know. But you can. You’re nearly through the year.”

Thomas nods. He seems calmer when Marcus leaves.

The next morning his bed is empty.


---

The Aftermath

The school responds with practised efficiency. A private funeral. A letter to parents emphasising pastoral care. Thomas’s name is not read at chapel. Within a fortnight the official position is grief, silence, and moving on.

Brother Declan gives a reading at the memorial.

He is dismissed later that term. Quietly. A mutual decision. He goes to another school.

Diana Webb, given just enough suggestion, shapes the rest.

Jake hears the story third-hand. It arrives filtered: Marcus as destabilising, as too close to Thomas, as a factor. Not an accusation. Something worse — an implication.

Jake does not believe it. Not entirely.

But he does not dismiss it either.

When Marcus tries to explain, he finds that grief has made him inarticulate. Jake listens, but his eyes have changed in a way Marcus cannot reach past.


---

The Separation

Marcus is moved. Diana requests it formally, citing associations and pastoral concerns. The school agrees.

He transfers to Alderton College.

Jake watches him go. They do not say a real goodbye.


---

The Separate Years

At Alderton, Marcus rebuilds slowly. The school is less cruel, though not kind. He finds space to breathe. He makes the first team. He does not make close friends. He writes letters to Jake that he does not send.

At St. Cormac’s, Jake has the year expected of him. He is better than ever on the pitch. Predicted top grades. Girls. Parties.

He is also increasingly volatile. He picks fights. He lies awake replaying the last real conversation he had with Marcus, trying to identify the exact moment he failed.


---

The Cup Final

May. A neutral pitch between the two schools. Thick spring mud. A grey afternoon that feels outside time.

They see each other during warm-up. Neither waves.

The match is brutal. Jake is extraordinary, which he usually is. Marcus matches him, which he did not always used to be able to do. They move in each other’s orbit, reading each other instinctively, colliding with more force than necessary.

Late in the second half, Jake goes down hard — a collision, breath knocked from him. The game pauses.

The Alderton physio jogs on. John Ellery. Thomas’s father.

He is practical, efficient. He kneels beside Jake, checks him, speaks in the calm tone of someone used to managing damage.

For a moment, they are alone in the noise.

John studies him briefly, recognition not quite formed, then says, almost absently:

“I thought they’d told you about that master of his. The one he was frightened of.”

Jake frowns, not fully processing.

John continues, still working, not looking at him:

“It wasn’t other boys. He was scared of that teacher. Kept asking to be moved out of those sessions.”

He says it as though it is known. As though it always has been.

The referee calls time. John stands, moves away.

The game resumes.


---

The Shift

Something has moved.

Jake plays differently. Not better, not worse — but as though something has been removed from between him and the world.

He looks across the pitch at Marcus, and for the first time in months, sees him without the distortion.

Marcus, later, will not know exactly when it changed. Only that something did.

The game goes to extra time. Then penalties.


---

The Moment

The final penalty is scored. The whistle goes.

For a second, there is nothing.

Then one of them moves. Later, neither will be certain who.

They walk toward each other across the mud.

They stop close enough to see clearly.

There is no speech. No explanation. No resolution of what has happened over the past year.

Only recognition.

They hold on too long.

And then — in the mud, in front of everyone, on a school football pitch in England in 1986 — they kiss.


---

The Ripping Apart

It lasts seconds.

Then the hands come — fathers, coaches — pulling, shouting, separating them with the violence of people afraid of what they are seeing.

The touchline is a wall of coats and noise.

They are dragged in opposite directions.

Jake twists back. Marcus is forced forward.

They see each other once more, both still catching their breath.


---

The Ending

The story ends there.

No reconciliation. No understanding from the world around them.

On poly telling and development/structure notes  :

This story has real power — the bones are exceptional. The institutional silence, Diana as a believable villain who genuinely loves her son, the Thomas thread as the load-bearing tragedy underneath everything else. The polyphonic first-person is exactly right for it: the dramatic irony becomes unbearable in the best way when readers understand what characters can't say to each other.

Let me work through the structural logic and then show you what the voices could sound like.

---

**The Core Structural Idea**

Think of it as a fugue. Each voice introduces its theme, then they develop in counterpoint. The reader assembles the truth that no single character possesses. Thomas's sections should get shorter and more syntactically fractured as the story progresses — his voice literally breaking down on the page — while Diana's sections get longer and more elaborately self-justifying, because she has more story to tell herself. Jake's voice is confident and concrete until it suddenly isn't. Marcus's is controlled, almost journalistic, watching everything, understanding too much and too late.

The dramatic irony engine: readers see Brother Declan through multiple perspectives simultaneously — Thomas's, Marcus's, the school's silence — and understand the whole before any single character does. This is what makes the Diana/Declan meeting so devastating: she goes to the one person she should not trust, and the reader watches it happen.

---

**The Voices**

**Jake** speaks in short declarative sentences, sensory and physical. He describes feelings by describing actions. When emotion surfaces he shifts register — becomes almost impatient, as though the words aren't behaving. He uses football as a displacement vocabulary. He's not unintelligent; he's avoidant, and the reader learns to hear the silences between his sentences.

**Marcus** is precise and watchful. Scholarship-boy hypervigilance: he notices everything because misreading a room has costs Jake will never have. His sentences are longer, more qualified. He thinks in conditionals. His sections feel like careful reports from someone who has learned that the gap between what you observe and what you're permitted to say is where you live.

**Thomas** is the brightest voice, initially — quick, warm, full of lateral connections between things. Latin quotes that land as jokes. Then the brightness starts flickering. His sections get shorter. A sentence starts and doesn't finish. He describes the school chapel ceiling in exact detail in a way that signals he is memorizing surfaces to stay inside them.

**Diana** is the most dangerous voice because she's compelling. She genuinely loves Marcus. Her self-narrative is fluent and internally consistent. She describes herself as a woman who acts. She never lies in her own head — she selects, she arranges, she curates. The reader has to do the work of seeing what she won't.

---

**Sample Passages — the opening weave**

---

*JAKE*

The thing about St. Cormac's is the smell. Floor polish and something older underneath. Incense, maybe, or damp stone. My father says it smells like ambition. My father went here in sixty-two. There's a photograph.

I arrived in September with a trunk that was too heavy and shoes that needed breaking in and the name Hartley, which meant something here. I didn't choose it to mean something. It just did.

The first time I saw Marcus Webb he was reading on the steps outside the chapel in the rain. Not sheltering, not rushing — reading, one hand keeping the page flat. I remember thinking: that's going to be expensive, that book.

I don't remember what I thought after that. Nothing worth noting.

---

*MARCUS*

Partial scholarship. They don't announce it but everyone knows. The teachers know, the boys know, the way the air changes slightly when the topic of school fees comes up in conversation. You learn to read those changes. I've always been good at that.

My mother dropped me at the gate. She straightened my tie in the car and said she was proud of me. Just that, without the usual modification — without *and I expect great things* or *don't let me down* or *this is a chance you must not waste*. Just: I'm proud of you.

I keep that sentence in a drawer in my head where I can look at it.

The boy on the pitch at warm-up that first week — Hartley — he played like he had never once been afraid. I found that extraordinary. Not the skill. The absence of fear. I didn't understand it yet. I filed it away.

---

*THOMAS*

Here is what nobody tells you about Latin: the word *amor* has no good plural. You can say *amores*, technically, but it sounds wrong, like a word stretched to fit something it wasn't made for. Catullus gets around this by just saying it over and over. *Odi et amo.* I hate and I love. As if saying them together is the only way to make them honest.

Brother Declan says I have a gift. He wrote it in red ink in my exercise book in September. He says it gently. He remembers my name even in corridors.

I told my mother in a letter. She wrote back and said she was glad I'd settled in.

I have settled in. It's an odd phrase. Like sediment.

---

**The Diana/Declan meeting — the pivot**

This is the scene where the story turns. It needs to live entirely inside Diana's head, and it needs to be almost completely wrong while feeling, to her, like clarity.

---

*DIANA*

I found it in December, folded inside a geography textbook on the shelf above his desk. Not a diary — he's never been a diary boy. Just pages. Questions, really, the kind you write to see if the words will tell you something your head won't.

I want to be clear: I wasn't snooping. I was tidying. There is a difference.

I read it twice. Then I sat on the edge of his bed and I thought about his father, who left when Marcus was six, and the way I had organized our life around ensuring that Marcus would never have to accommodate weakness — mine or anyone else's. I thought about the school, which costs more than I have, which I've managed by categories of sacrifice I don't name because naming them makes them real.

And I thought: not this. Not after everything.

I made an appointment the first week of January. The train to Chertsey, a taxi, the gate, the porter who looked at me in the way they do — assessing what my clothes mean, filing the answer incorrectly.

Brother Declan has an excellent office. Books in Latin and Greek, a wooden crucifix, a reading lamp that throws warm light. He listens with his whole body, slightly forward. He is the kind of man who makes you feel you are being understood.

He chose his words carefully. He said: *some friendships, in a place like this, can become — intense. In ways that aren't always helpful. For either boy.*

He said: *Marcus is a sensitive boy. Bright, certainly. But sensitive.*

He said he would take a closer pastoral interest. He said it with such particular care that I felt, for a moment, that someone was finally helping me.

I thanked him. I took the taxi back to the station.

I told myself I had not made anything worse.

I believed it.

---

**Thomas's fracturing — three sections across the middle of the story**

These should be separated by other voices. The gap between them is where the horror lives.

---

*THOMAS [earlier]*

Jake Hartley asked me tonight what the Latin for *loyal* was and I said *fidelis* and he said that sounded like a dog's name and I said that was the point, actually, dogs were the example, and he said *oh* in the way he does when something has landed that he didn't expect. He was thinking about Marcus. He didn't say so. He didn't need to.

I think he thinks I don't notice things. I notice everything. It's a habit I can't stop.

---

*THOMAS [middle]*

Brother Declan says I am his best student. He says this privately. He has a particular way of saying things privately — a door closed, a tone lowered, a hand.

I have started writing things down and then crossing them out so completely the words can't be read. I don't know who I think might find them. I just know I can't have them exist legibly in the world.

The chapel ceiling has twelve panels. I can tell you what's in each one. I've had some time to look at it.

---

*THOMAS [last, before the bed is empty]*

M—

I keep starting this and not

The thing I wanted to say was about the Latin. *Odi et amo.* I think he had it right. I think it means: I am two things at once and both of them are true and there is no word for what that makes you.

I don't think this school has a word for it either.

I wanted to ask you something but I think the answer might be

---

**The match — John Ellery's one section**

Give him a single section, placed just before the Jake/Marcus reunion. Short. Plain. Like a door left open by accident.

---

*JOHN*

I've worked with school teams for twelve years. You learn to read boys quickly — not their skill, that's obvious enough. The other thing. Whether they're carrying something.

Thomas carried it for almost a full term before the end. His mother and I have discussed, many times, what we saw and what we should have done differently. These discussions don't resolve.

I took the Alderton physio job in January. I didn't tell anyone from his old school. I didn't think I had anything to say to them.

Then in May there was a boy on the pitch with the wrong name attached to him, and he was down in the mud in front of me, and he was the age Thomas would have been, and I looked at his face and I knew — the way you know things at that point that you cannot prove — that someone had told him a version of a story that wasn't right.

I said what I knew. Plainly. Then I stood up and let the game continue.

I don't know if it was enough. I have stopped expecting to know that.

---

**Structural notes for the full draft**

The sections should be labeled only with a name, not a date or chapter number — this creates the sense of simultaneous testimony. Let readers do the chronological assembly.

Withhold Diana's section until after you've shown Thomas's fracturing. The juxtaposition — her self-justifying clarity arriving after his fragmenting voice — is where the story becomes almost unbearable.

Jake should have one section where he's describing the match using only football language, and it should be obvious to the reader that he's describing something else entirely.

The final section — the moment and its aftermath — could either be Jake alone, or you could give each of them one last short paragraph, same event, same seconds, different interior. The last line then becomes a kind of chorus: four voices arriving at it from different angles.

The current final line is very strong. Keep it. But consider letting Thomas have the very last word — a fragment from one of those crossed-out letters, surfaced at the end like something that didn't stay buried.

Just two boys who loved each other in a world that had no place for it — and the knowledge, arrived too late, that they had been separated by something that was never true.

Somewhere in it is Thomas. And the laugh that made a room warmer. And the thing he tried to say that nobody heard correctly.

And the adults — one who distorted, one who spoke plainly — and the difference that made, and didn’t make.

The last line:

They smashed it. But it wasn’t the way they said.  

Based on the structure, style, and comparable works, here's the honest breakdown.

---

**The estimate: 75,000–90,000 words. Target the middle — 80,000.**

---

**Why not longer**

The restraint is load-bearing. The fragmented, polyphonic structure — voices that don't explain themselves, silences that do the work — compresses naturally. Every word Thomas *doesn't* finish is a word you don't write. Diana's self-deception lands harder in 1,800 words than 3,500. This isn't a sprawling novel. Its power comes from precision.

Going to 120,000+ would require subplots, extended world-building, or an aftermath section that would almost certainly dilute the ending you already have.

---

**Why not shorter**

Below 70,000 and the voices don't have room to develop their idioms fully before they start converging. Readers need long enough with Jake's displacement vocabulary, and Marcus's conditional thinking, that when those patterns break — they feel it. The fugue structure requires time to establish the themes before it can complicate them.

---

**Rough section breakdown**

| Voice | Sections | Avg length | Subtotal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jake | 10–12 | 1,800 words | ~20,000 |
| Marcus | 10–12 | 2,000 words | ~22,000 |
| Thomas | 7–8 | 600 words | ~4,500 |
| Diana | 5–6 | 2,200 words | ~12,000 |
| John Ellery | 1–2 | 700 words | ~1,000 |
| Interludes/transitions | — | — | ~5,000 |

That puts the core narrative at roughly **65,000 words**, with the remainder absorbed by scene-setting within sections, the institutional texture of the school, and the match sequence which probably needs more room than the outline suggests.

---

**Comparable novels**

- *Never Let Me Go* — Ishiguro — 105,000 words (similar institutional dread, similar restraint but more expansive)
- *A Separate Peace* — Knowles — 59,000 words (too compressed for what you're doing with four voices)
- *Atonement* — McEwan — 123,000 words (more architecturally ambitious, longer aftermath)
- *The Remains of the Day* — Ishiguro — 86,000 words (closest tonal equivalent — unreliable interiority, institutional setting, devastation through what isn't said)

The Remains of the Day comparison is the most useful. Same emotional economy. That's your ceiling and your model.

---

**Practical note**

The draft you have maps to roughly 3,500 words of outline. A 1:20–1:25 expansion ratio to finished prose is normal for literary fiction at this density. That math also lands at 70,000–87,000 words.

80,000. That's the number to write toward.

# Writing Guide
## *St. Cormac's* — A Working Document

A full-build companion for the polyphonic novel outlined in your draft. Use this alongside the outline, not instead of it. The outline tells you what happens. This tells you how to write it without losing what makes it work.

---

## 1. Premise & Promise

Before anything else, lock the thing the book is for. Everything below serves it.

**The premise:** Four voices, one institution, one summer of consequence. A boy is abused, a mother intervenes wrongly, another boy dies, two other boys are separated by a story that is not true. They meet again in the mud, briefly, and are torn apart.

**The promise to the reader:** Dramatic irony as a moral instrument. The reader will assemble the truth that no character possesses, and will feel the cost of every silence. The kiss is not a payoff. The understanding is the payoff. The kiss is what the world refuses to allow them to keep.

**What the book is *not*:** A coming-of-age. A romance. A trauma narrative in the confessional sense. A whodunit about Brother Declan (the reader knows almost from the first Thomas section). A story with redemption.

If you find a scene drifting toward any of those, the scene is wrong, not the structure.

---

## 2. Structural Architecture: The Fugue, Operationalised

The fugue analogy is correct but it needs concrete machinery or it stays decorative.
