essays.title: Marcus
essays.body:
My mother bought the shoes in Reading two days before term began, from a shop that had no proper boys’ department but did have a man who called her madam in a way she found reassuring.  They were black, too bright, and stiff across the toes. I knew as soon as he brought them from the back room that they were wrong. Not wrong in themselves. They were good shoes, probably better than I had any right to object to, and I could see her doing the calculation before she asked the price: whether they would last a year if I polished them properly, whether a year was too hopeful, whether she could stretch the housekeeping by not replacing her own winter coat, whether saying yes too quickly would make the assistant understand that the decision had cost something.
“They’ll do very well,” she said.
The assistant bent down with the shoehorn. “A little room in them. He’ll grow.”
I did not say that I had mostly stopped growing. Mothers liked room in things. Shoes, blazers, expectations. If a thing was bought too large, it meant the future had been included in the price.
“They’re smart,” she said to me on the pavement outside, as though I had accused them of something.
“They are.”
“Not too smart.”
“No.”
“You mustn’t go ruining them straightaway.”
“I won’t.”
That was not, strictly speaking, a promise I was in any position to keep. St Cormac’s ruined things. Shoes, handwriting, accents if you let it, though the accent was complicated because the school did not so much remove yours as make you aware of it until you began cutting pieces away yourself. My mother heard those cuts when I came home. She never remarked on them directly. She would say, “You sound tired,” or “They do speak very properly there,” and I would say nothing, because to answer either way was to admit to an adjustment.
On the morning I went back, she stood in the hall with my scarf over one arm and brushed my shoulders with her hand, though there was nothing on them. She had always done that before departures: removed invisible lint, straightened invisible error. The house was still dark at the edges because the sky outside had not fully committed to morning. The kettle ticked in the kitchen. My trunk waited beside the door, brown leather, cracked at one corner, polished more carefully than was sensible.
“You have your envelopes?”
“Yes.”
“And stamps?”
“Yes.”
“Not all at once this time.”
“I know.”
“I mean, don’t use them all writing to me the first week and then none at all.”
“I won’t.”
She lifted the scarf and put it round my neck. It was new, though she did not say so. Blue stripes, narrow, regular. Not St Cormac’s colours, which were black and white and a red that had darkened almost to dried blood on the older boards. I think she had chosen blue because it looked harmless. Respectable without imitating. She was good at those distinctions.
“You don’t have to wear it once you’re there,” she said.
“All right.”
“But you might until you go in.”
“All right.”
She stepped back to look at me.
There were things she wanted to say then. I could see them arriving and being refused. My mother had a face that did not hide effort well, which was one reason I learned to hide mine. She wanted, I think, to ask whether I was happy there. Not whether I was doing well. Doing well had figures attached to it: marks, sets, team lists, reports with phrases like conscientious and promising, which could be folded and kept. Happiness was vaguer and therefore dangerous. If she asked and I said yes, she would suspect I was protecting her. If I said no, she would have to decide whether protection was worth the cost of taking me away.
So she said, “Make sure you keep up.”
It would have sounded harsh to someone who did not know her. I knew exactly what it meant. Keep up with work. Keep up with boys whose fathers bought new trunks without discussing it. Keep up with jokes you had to understand quickly. Keep up with the football, because in a place like St Cormac’s football was not a game so much as a passport office. Keep up with Jake Crayford, though she did not say his name.
“I will,” I said.
She nodded, as if that settled the matter between us and the world.
We took the train part of the way and then the school coach from the station, though not one of the large coaches used for away fixtures. This was a smaller vehicle smelling of cold vinyl, petrol, and boys who had been made to say goodbye in public. My mother did not come on the coach. She stood on the station forecourt while the driver loaded trunks. I watched her from the window after I sat down. She had one gloved hand raised, not waving exactly, just held there. I raised mine back and then looked away before the coach moved, because I had learned that departures were easier if one behaved as though they had already happened.
St Cormac’s appeared gradually. First the upper trees above the road, bare and black against a bright winter sky; then the chapel tower, too square to be beautiful and too old to be dismissed; then the lodge, the gravel, the slope of wet grass climbing to the main buildings. New boys always looked up when the tower came into view. Older boys pretended not to, which was another way of looking.
By the time I reached Rambton House, my shoes had already begun to hurt.
I had arrived early because my mother believed lateness exposed need. The house door had been open, so I carried my trunk into the hall and put it under the stairs before anyone could tell me where to put it. That was one of the small advantages of returning: not belonging, exactly, but knowing the correct place for a thing before being instructed. Brother Andrew passed me once and said, “Mr Webb,” in acknowledgement rather than greeting. I said, “Brother,” and he continued to the office with his papers held against his chest as if they might otherwise escape.
The hall was not yet full. It had the waiting smell of a school building before boys occupy it completely: polish, dust, coal smoke from somewhere old in the walls, a faint medicinal trace from Matron’s room. Rambton’s entrance alcove caught the morning light through the high window, so I sat there at the top of the steps, just outside the main door, because it allowed me to see the drive without seeming to be waiting for anyone.
That distinction mattered.
If I sat inside, I was early. If I stood outside, I was anxious. Sitting in the alcove meant I could pretend I had chosen the light.
I had a book with me, but I did not read it. I opened it at a page I had already read twice and kept my thumb in the margin. Boys arrived in clumps. Some had fathers who shook hands too hard and said things like “Right, then” because tenderness embarrassed them. Some had mothers who kissed them in front of the steps and thereby destroyed them for several days. Some were delivered by drivers and emerged without looking back, which seemed enviable until one noticed that no one had looked at them either.
I noticed shoes. One could tell quite a lot from shoes. New shoes with confidence were different from new shoes with apology. Old shoes could be careless or poor depending on how they had been maintained. Jake’s shoes, when he came, would be good and badly treated, because he had always had the peculiar freedom of someone who could damage expensive things without the damage becoming evidence.
I saw his trunk first.
It came up the steps at an angle, knocking his knee because he was carrying it too fast and with more strength than patience. Then I saw him behind it, hair blown from the walk up, face bright from the cold, mouth already arranged around whatever he had decided to say. Jake did not enter a place so much as take the first yard of it.
I had known I would be pleased to see him. That was reasonable. We had shared a dorm, played together all last term, and there are not many boys at St Cormac’s with whom one can be silent without the silence becoming a contest. Still, the amount of relief was disproportionate. It arrived physically, before thought: a loosening under the ribs, a ridiculous lift in the throat, as if some part of the morning had been holding itself until he appeared.
It irritated me. Not him. The relief.
“All right?” he said.
“All right.”
That was safe. Two words was the correct size for pleasure between boys. More than that and one risked making a display of it.
He dropped the trunk beside me and it struck the stone with enough force to make a first year’s mother glance over. Jake did not notice. He rarely noticed the first consequence of a thing if he was already moving toward the second.
“You’ve packed bricks,” I said.
“Training regime.”
“For whom?”
“Porters.”
He looked at me then, properly, and I smiled because not smiling would have been stranger. The winter sun was in his eyes, so he narrowed them, and the expression made him seem both older and more exactly himself. He was still carrying Austria with him. Snow, speed, air, whatever expensive boys brought back from mountains and expected the rest of us to understand by enthusiasm alone.
“Kolsters good?” I asked.
“Brilliant.”
“You’ve mentioned it.”
“I haven’t.”
“You have now.”
“That’s once.”
“You wrote it on the card.”
“That doesn’t count.”
I had the card in my blazer pocket. I am not sure why I had brought it back with me. It would have been more sensible to leave it at home in the drawer with letters, reports, and other things that had to be kept flat and unhandled. The front showed a white slope under a blue sky, the kind of blue English winters only achieved in advertisements. On the back he had written: Snow brilliant. You’d die. Jake.
I had read it more times than its contents justified.
One reason was that Jake had written it at all. Another was that it gave evidence of a life happening elsewhere: his family, their holiday, a mountain village with a name I had not known how to pronounce when my mother asked. It should perhaps have made me feel excluded. It did, a little. But mostly it had made him less absent.
“You should have come,” he said.
“Yes. Well.”
I looked at my shoes because they offered an exit. There were things one could explain and things one could only place quietly between oneself and another person. We did not go skiing. We did not have spare money for international accidents. My mother would not have known what to do with an invitation from the Crayfords even if one had been offered sincerely, which it had not been. Jake said you should have come in the same tone he might say you should have shot first time, as though the failure had been tactical.
The great door opened behind us and the house breathed out.
Jake turned toward it at once. He always looked at buildings as if they owed him something, and in this case perhaps they did. Rambton held his father’s name in gold. His grandfather’s presence was in other places, if not as visible. He knew where to stand under inherited things. I knew how not to be seen looking at them.
Inside, the hall was gathering itself into term. Trunks, coats, shouted surnames, the high clatter of wooden hangers being knocked together in the cloakroom. A second year dragged a trunk backwards and nearly clipped my ankle. He apologised toward Jake.
That was not unusual enough to be remarkable, and yet I remarked it.
The boy had seen both of us. He had endangered my ankle. He apologised to Jake because Jake was the person in the scene to whom apology naturally travelled. I do not mean he did it maliciously. Most arrangements are not malicious. They simply reveal where gravity is.
Jake saw the house board.
Of course he did. He always did, though I think he believed he was discreet. His father’s name was painted there twice. A.J. Crayford, Football Captain, 1962. A.J. Crayford, Head of House, 1962. I knew the letters because I had read them often enough, not from admiration but from needing to understand which names altered the weather. Crayford altered it. Hale altered it on a smaller, uglier scale. Webb did not alter anything.
“You’ll wear the letters off staring at them,” I said.
“I’m checking they haven’t made a mistake.”
“They haven’t.”
“They might.”
“They seem fairly committed to the error.”
He grinned. I was pleased with myself for that, though I did not show it. With Jake one could sometimes be clever quickly enough that cleverness became part of the game rather than a separate thing. With other boys, cleverness had to be rationed. Too much of it drew attention, and attention was rarely neutral.
We carried his trunk together down the hall. He did not ask me to help. I simply took one end. There are forms of friendship that depend on not asking for what one expects to be given. That sounds unkind, but it is not always. Jake expected help the way some people expect doors to open. It had not yet occurred to him that this expectation might be a form of wealth.
Hale came out of the boot room.
I knew before he spoke that he would choose the shoes. His eyes went there first, then to my scarf, then to Jake. Hale’s face had an economy to it. He disliked whatever did not strengthen his position and inspected people for uses or weaknesses. I had watched him last term reduce a first year to tears by asking three questions about his father’s car.
“Crayford,” he said. “Webb.”
Jake answered first. He always did when danger had shape.
“Hale.”
“New pair, Webb?”
The temptation was to look down. I did not. It is usually a mistake to verify an insult for the person making it.
“Careful with them,” Hale said. “Rambton stairs eat little London shoes.”
“He’s from Reading,” Jake said.
I could not tell whether gratitude or embarrassment came first. They were so close together that the distinction may be false. I had not needed rescuing. That was what I told myself. Hale was lazy, and lazy cruelty rarely pursued silence for long. Yet Jake had intervened without calculation, and the room shifted because he had. His words were not especially clever. They were not even entirely useful. But they placed him beside me, and that placement mattered.
“He’s from Reading,” he said, as if factual correction were a form of tackle.
“I don’t care where he’s from.”
“Then why ask?”
“I didn’t.”
“You sort of did.”
The hall made its small circle around them. It was not obvious; masters like to believe they are the only people who can command silence, but boys create it faster. Hale took one step in, performing decision. Jake’s shoulders changed. He did not become larger exactly, but more available to impact.
Brother Andrew arrived with his papers.
“Gentlemen.”
The word struck all of us equally and therefore saved everyone without appearing to save anyone. Brother Andrew had that ability. He could prevent a fight while leaving each boy with his preferred version of why the fight had not happened.
After Hale moved on, Brother Andrew assigned us to dormitory four. Same corridor. Trunks outside until inspection. No contraband food. He looked at Jake when he said that. Jake lied in the easy way of boys whose lies have often been treated as energy rather than offence.
“I haven’t got any.”
I knew at once he had. Not because I had seen it, but because the denial had pleasure in it.
Brother Andrew turned to me.
“Mr Webb?”
“No, Brother.”
That answer had no pleasure. It had accuracy, which is safer and less liked.
When we reached the common room, the fire smoked sideways and several boys pretended smoke was a matter of character. The photograph on the mantelpiece had been cleaned over the holiday, or perhaps I only noticed it because Jake went directly to it. Last year’s senior eleven. Duncan Closh with the cup. Eddy Smith beside him. Both certain to move up, according to the arithmetic of boys who cared about teams before timetables.
Jake stood in front of it as if reading a prophecy.
“Second XI by Christmas,” he said.
“That soon?”
“You don’t think?”
“I didn’t say that.”
“You looked like that.”
“How does one look like that?”
“Like you’re thinking too much.”
“I was thinking that Closh has enormous knees.”
This was partly true. Closh’s knees were indeed enormous, pale even in the photograph, somehow more prominent than his face. But the other thought, the one I did not offer, was that Jake’s confidence had a danger in it because it made the world feel briefly obliged to comply. If he said Second XI by Christmas, one wanted it to be so. I wanted it to be so, not merely for myself. For him. For the shape his face would take when the list went up, for the way he would pretend not to care and then talk of nothing else for two days.
That was another disproportionate thing.
Thomas Ellery sat on the window ledge with Catullus.
Thomas made occupation look accidental. He could sit in a room full of noise and give the impression that the room had arranged itself around his reading rather than the reverse. He was smaller than many of us, too thin at the wrists, with a face that seemed unfinished until he smiled; then it became suddenly quick and precise, as if someone had lit a lamp behind it.
“Crayford. Webb. Survivors return.”
“Of what?” Jake said.
“The holidays. Obviously. Some boys never recover from proximity to family.”
Thomas liked sentences that turned on their own heels. Jake liked them when he understood them quickly enough to catch the turn.
“What are you reading?” I asked.
“Catullus.”
“Again?”
“Still. There’s a difference.”
He held the book as though the difference mattered. It probably did. Thomas had a way of making distinctions feel less like showing off than hospitality. He would offer you some small precision — still, not again; translation, not meaning; Rome, not Latin — and wait to see whether you wanted to step inside it.
Jake asked about Kolsters as though everyone’s relation to mountains was a personal failing.
“You should come next year. Snow’s unbelievable.”
“I am built for libraries and light drizzle,” Thomas said. “Mountains would expose me.”
“To what?”
“Gravity.”
I laughed before judging whether laughter was wise. It came out cleanly, which embarrassed me more than if it had been loud. Jake glanced at me. Not long. Just enough to register it.
Then the room moved toward the football notice.
One learns in school how to read movement before speech. A group at the far wall, a shout, then the surge. Jake was through it at once, not rudely exactly but without apology. I followed because if one hesitated one became part of the obstruction.
The notice was in Abbot Holsworth’s hand.
Football Trials — Lent Term.
Senior squads: Tuesday fortnight.
Middle school preliminary: Thursday.
All boys to attend unless excused by medical certificate.
Names below. First XI likely. Second XI possible. Third XI retained.
Jake’s name under Second XI possible.
Mine beneath it.
It is difficult to explain the pressure a list can exert on the body. Adults think lists announce information. At St Cormac’s they altered rank. A boy not named became smaller for the rest of the day. A boy named under possible became visible in a way that might be promise or threat. I felt both. There was pleasure, yes, but it arrived already compromised by the knowledge that possible meant being watched. If one failed privately, one remained private. If one failed after being named, failure acquired witnesses.
“See?” Jake said.
“Possible.”
“That means likely.”
“It means possible.”
“It means don’t be a clerk.”
“My father is a clerk.”
I did not intend to say it. The sentence came out before I could make it gentler, and once spoken it sat between us with all its small furniture: my father’s work, Jake’s ignorance, my irritation, my wish not to have displayed either.
Jake’s face changed. Not much, but enough. His confidence stalled, as if he had put a foot down and found no ground.
“I didn’t mean—”
“I know.”
I said it too quickly because I wanted the moment over. The problem with class at school was that any acknowledgement of it made one look as if one had brought it in oneself. Better to move on. Better to accept the joke as a joke, the slight as accidental, the rescue as unnecessary, the list as fair, the room as neutral.
Jake punched my arm.
“Second XI possible. You’re buying tuck when it happens.”
“I don’t have any money.”
“You can owe me.”
“I already owe you.”
“You do?”
“For the sherbet lemons last term.”
“Those were tactical supplies.”
“For what?”
“Latin.”
“We had geography.”
“Same building.”
It was clumsy and kind and worked because he intended it to. That is one of the things I noticed about Jake very early, though I did not put it in those terms then. He often damaged things by accident, but he also repaired by instinct. The repairs were not always sufficient. Sometimes they were not repairs at all, merely new damage laid over old. But they came quickly, and one forgave speed more easily than thought.
The handbell rang for lunch.
We crossed the quad in the loose order of returning boys. I saw the first years first, because I had been one recently enough to remember the posture: heads slightly forward, hands uncertain, eyes trying to take everything in without appearing to look. One of them had been kissed by his mother in the hall. He would have two difficult days now. Not because the kiss meant anything shameful in itself, but because tenderness, once witnessed, could be used by anyone.
Jake said, “Dead by Evensong.”
“Probably homesick.”
“That’s what I said.”
“No. You said dead.”
“Same thing first week.”
He said it easily, but I heard the old truth under it. The first week did kill something in most boys. Not dramatically. No one marked the death. A boy learned not to cry where sound carried, not to ask questions whose answers everyone else seemed to know, not to look too long at someone else’s letter from home, not to be the last to understand a joke. By the second week he had become more convenient. Adults called this settling in.
The war memorial stood dark in the centre of the quad. I slowed to read it, as I always did. Names were safer than faces. They did not look back and ask what business one had noticing them. The older names had been cut more deeply, or perhaps weather had made them seem so. Boys had once stood here, or near here, and then later their names had returned without them. St Cormac’s was very good at preserving names. It was less clear to me what it did with boys.
Jake did not slow. He knew one of the names without needing to read it. That is a different relation to memory.
Lunch was beef, which made everyone cheerful in the exaggerated way boarding school food can briefly make boys cheerful. The dining hall held the smell of gravy, boiled cabbage, old wood, and damp wool warming under bodies. We sat at Rambton table, third years placed where third years belonged, neither ignored nor important.
Abbot Holsworth was at high table.
I saw him see Jake. The nod was almost nothing, which is to say it was exactly enough. Jake sat straighter as if a string had been pulled through his spine. I do not know whether he knew he had done it. It would have been kinder if he did not.
“What?” he said.
“Nothing.”
“It was a nod.”
“I didn’t say it wasn’t.”
“It means something.”
“It may mean he has a neck.”
“You’re jealous.”
“Of his neck?”
“Of my football future.”
“Vastly.”
I said it lightly. Underneath, I was thinking that Jake’s future seemed to come toward him with adults already nodding. Mine did not. Mine had to be approached carefully, in the right shoes, with the correct envelopes and no visible appetite.
After lunch came chapel.
First-day chapel had a particular cruelty because it gathered boys at the moment they were least prepared to be gathered. We were still full of noise from arrival, still carrying the afterimage of home, still testing whether friendships had survived the holiday. Then the chapel took us and made us kneel.
It was colder than the quad. The air held wax, stone, incense, and the dry paper smell of hymnals handled by generations of boys who had sung badly and grown up anyway. The crucifix above the altar looked paler in winter light. I had never known where to put my eyes during chapel. Looking down seemed furtive. Looking up seemed theatrical. Looking straight ahead meant seeing the back of another boy’s neck for twenty minutes and learning more about him than either of you wanted.
Brother Declan read the lesson.
I liked Brother Declan. That was the simplest version, though simple versions are rarely complete. He taught Latin as if the language were a set of doors rather than a wall. He did not shout often. He corrected with red ink and a dry patience that made one want to be accurate for reasons beyond marks. Boys who disliked Latin still liked being seen by him. That was a power too, though I did not yet think of it that way.
“Charity suffereth long, and is kind.”
Behind us someone whispered, “suffereth wrong,” and swallowed laughter. Brother Declan did not look up. His not looking up had more authority than another master’s glare.
Jake glanced sideways at me. I was looking at the prayer book but not reading. His knee moved once against the pew, impatient. Chapel did that to him. Stillness made his body argue.
Thomas was two places down, beyond Perry, mouthing the words half a beat before they arrived. I noticed because Thomas did that with many things: anticipated the line, the joke, the correction, sometimes even the hurt. It made him seem quick. It may also have made him tired.
Father Anselm spoke about character.
He said new terms were new mercies. He said boys became men through obedience to ordinary duties. He said St Cormac’s did not exist to produce cleverness or success, though both were welcome, but character.
I wrote the sentence down in my head because one had to collect such sentences. They explained what adults thought they were doing. Character, in their mouths, meant the part of you that remained after discomfort had been given a moral purpose. If you complained, you lacked it. If you endured, they had built it. This was a closed system and therefore hard to argue against.
The hymn was “Praise to the Holiest.” Perry sang with astonishing commitment and no evidence of pitch. Jake’s mouth twitched twice. I kept mine still.
After chapel, sound returned as if a lid had been lifted from boiling water.
Dormitory four was ours again. Eight beds. Cream metal frames. Window over the small pitch. The same cupboard door that did not shut unless kicked at the bottom. The same radiator that worked only when no one needed it. I took the bed opposite Jake’s because it was the one I had had before and because it allowed conversation in the dark without turning one’s head too obviously.
Matron inspected trunks.
Jake’s trunk looked, from the outside, like something meant for a boy whose possessions were expected to travel well. Inside it was disorderly enough to be reassuring. Boots, shirts, books, socks, a games bag not quite closed, and under the boots the chocolate he had denied owning.
“That is not mine,” he said when Matron found it.
“It is in your trunk, Mr Crayford.”
“Someone’s framed me.”
“With six bars of Dairy Milk?”
“Ambitious frame.”
He enjoyed Matron and she, despite herself, enjoyed him. Some boys made adults forgive them before they had finished misbehaving. It was a talent, and like most talents it could look like innocence from a distance.
Then Matron opened my trunk.
I had packed it three times. Once alone, once after my mother checked whether I had remembered towels, and once again after she went to bed because her checking had altered the order. Shirts squared. Socks paired. Books stacked flat. Envelopes at the side. Tin of polish wrapped in an old cloth. No food. No magazine. No private thing that could be held up and made into public evidence.
“Very good, Mr Webb,” Matron said.
The praise landed wrongly. I wanted it, of course. That was the humiliating part. I wanted every adult sentence that suggested I had succeeded in making myself acceptable. But in front of Jake, good packing looked like obedience, and obedience was perilously close to fear.
Thomas appeared in the doorway and saved me from my own trunk.
“Contraband?”
“No,” Jake said.
Thomas leaned round as if entering a scene by punctuation rather than movement. “Webb packs like a novice monk.”
“Thank you,” I said.
“It wasn’t praise.”
“It sounded restful.”
That pleased him. I saw it in the quick narrowing of his eyes before Matron expelled him back to his own dormitory.
By late afternoon the house had settled into the complicated unreality of the first day back. Nothing had properly begun, but everything had resumed. Boys moved through corridors looking both older and exactly as they had before. Holiday stories were spent too quickly, then repeated. New haircuts were inspected. New bruises invented. Letters were put away. Sweets were negotiated. The school drew us back into its categories with a competence that would have been impressive if it had not been so complete.
Jake wanted to go out.
He did not say, “I want to go out.” He appeared with boots, ball, and a look that assumed my agreement. I might have refused, in theory. In practice the sight of the small pitch through the window had already done its work.
We were not properly changed. Boots over school socks, coats over uniforms. This was not allowed, but in the hierarchy of offences it was barely visible. St Cormac’s punished disobedience most severely when disobedience embarrassed authority. A few boys on a muddy pitch before supper embarrassed no one unless a window broke.
The ground was wet and good. The kind of January surface that seemed fast until it betrayed you. Jake loved those conditions because they rewarded conviction. I liked them because they made reading the ball more important than strength. Mud slowed the larger boys by a fraction, and fractions are where smaller advantages live.
Perry came. Closh’s younger brother came. Two second years hovered until Jake included them by throwing one the ball and saying, “You’re skins,” although nobody was taking shirts off in that cold. The boys accepted this as appointment.
Jake took the middle.
I went left.
There are forms of communication easier to survive than speech. Football was one. With Jake, especially, the pitch removed several dangers. He did not have to explain himself; I did not have to qualify myself. He moved and I understood the line. I moved and he sent the ball before my hand lifted. It was not magic, although boys liked to call it that when they wanted to make work invisible. We had learned one another’s habits through repetition: his tendency to cut inside if challenged square, my tendency to go early if the defender watched the ball, his refusal to give up a run once begun, my preference for passing low because school pitches made high balls stupid.
Still, there were moments when learned things felt like trust.
He took the ball from Perry, turned past Closh, and passed into space before I called. I was already there. I touched it back hard and low. He struck first time and put it wide.
“Should score,” I said.
“Pitch bobbled.”
“Air bobbled?”
“Shut up.”
This was happiness, I think, although I would not have used the word. At the time I understood it as rhythm. Breath hurting cleanly. Cold in the hands. Mud accepting us without inquiry. Jake shouting too much. The ball arriving where it ought to. My new shoes forgotten because my boots were old and trustworthy.
I scored from an angle I should not have tried. It clipped the inside of one coat and spun in. I was surprised, and Jake saw that.
“Fluke.”
“Obviously.”
“Try it again.”
“No.”
“Coward.”
“Strategic restraint.”
He laughed then, and for a moment the earlier feeling returned: that disproportionate gladness, the sense that seeing him pleased had somehow become part of my own balance. It was not exactly admiration. I admired some things about him and not others. It was not dependence either; I disliked dependence and monitored myself for signs of it. It was nearer to recognition, perhaps, though that word sounds too adult and too clean.
I only knew that when he was there the school became less dense.
That should have been ordinary. Boys have friends. Boys are pleased to see their friends after holidays. Boys play football and laugh and pass without thinking. The troubling part was not the fact of it, but the excess. I had been pleased to see Perry too, in a mild way, and Thomas, in a sharper way because Thomas made rooms more interesting. With Jake the feeling had weight. It had arrived before permission.
I put it aside because there was a ball to win.
The church bell rang for supper.
Everyone stopped. Even Jake, though he would never have admitted the bell had command over his muscles. It came from the bell house beside the church, deep enough to seem less struck than released. The sound moved through the grass, the wet brick, the bodies of boys cooling too quickly after running.
Jake looked at my shoes when we changed back.
“You’ll catch it from Matron.”
“They’re shoes.”
“They were shoes.”
He was right. The polish had gone at the edges and mud had dried along the welt. My mother would notice when I went home at half-term if I failed to repair them properly. She noticed wear the way other people noticed weather.
“My mother will mind,” I said.
“Tell her football happened.”
“That would not help.”
“No?”
“No.”
He did not understand, but to his credit he did not mock it. I could see him reaching for some response and failing to find one. Then he kicked the ball toward me, which was often how he solved discomfort. I trapped it badly on purpose because sometimes one has to give a friend the shape of normality back.
We walked in through the cold with mud on our boots and the light going. The chapel windows glowed. The house boards, when we reached Rambton, caught the last of the interior yellow. Jake looked up again at his father’s name.
I stopped because he had stopped.
“What?” he said.
“Nothing.”
“You’re doing it again.”
“Doing what?”
“Looking.”
“So are you.”
“That’s different.”
“How?”
“It’s my board.”
He said it quickly, proudly, without thinking. I looked at the names. Not all of them Crayfords, obviously. But his claim was not legal; it was atmospheric. He belonged to the board because the board had already made room for him. Even his uncertainty about living up to it was a form of inheritance.
“Is it?” I asked.
I should not have. It was too precise a question for the moment. Jake had no answer ready, and unanswered questions can feel like accusations even when they are not intended that way.
Hale saved him, if that is the word, by shouldering past.
“Move, possibles.”
The plural was designed well. Not Crayford. Not Webb. Possibles. It reduced the list to a joke and dragged us both into it, though not equally. Jake stepped after him. I saw the decision before it became action: jaw set, shoulders forward, the old pleasure of impact presenting itself as justice.
I put my hand on his sleeve.
Only for a second.
“Leave it,” I said.
He could have ignored me. In fact I expected him to, which made the pause more startling. Hale continued into the hall. Jake stayed where he was.
Then the moment passed and we went in.
I thought about that at supper more than I thought about the stew.
My hand on his sleeve had been nothing. Boys pulled, shoved, tackled, collided, leaned across one another daily. Touch was not rare. But that sort of touch, brief and asking rather than taking, was less common. I had done it before thinking because I knew the line of him so well in that instant: another half-second and he would be committed; another boy laughing and the whole term might begin with a fight; another master entering at the wrong angle and Jake’s name in a punishment book beneath Hale’s, which would somehow damage Jake more because adults expected better from names already painted in gold.
He left it because I asked.
That should also have been ordinary.
After supper there were house prayers, notices, the slow administrative dullness by which schools turn boys into entries. Matron returned Jake’s chocolate on the condition that it was shared. He complained enough to prove he did not mind. Thomas acquired two squares by theological argument and one by theft. Perry asked whether Catullus had ever played football, and Thomas said, “Spiritually, Perry, every Roman poet was a goalkeeper,” which kept us going for longer than it deserved.
In the corridor before bed, I saw Brother Declan speaking to Thomas outside dormitory six. Nothing dramatic. A master, a boy, a hand resting lightly on the doorframe. Thomas looking up, smiling at something said quietly. I remember it because Thomas’s smile was different there: smaller, less thrown outward. Or perhaps I only think that now. Memory is not a ledger, however much schools try to make life into one.
At the time I noticed and did nothing with the noticing.
Dormitory four became dark in stages. First the main light off, then whispering, then Perry told to shut up, then the corridor light still lying under the door, then rain against the window. Thin rain, steady enough to make the glass sound occupied.
I lay opposite Jake and listened to the room arrange itself into sleep.
Sleeping in a dormitory is an education in other people’s bodies. Breath, blankets, coughs swallowed or not swallowed, the small panicked movements of boys dreaming badly, the exaggerated stillness of boys pretending not to. Privacy at St Cormac’s was not absent; it existed in narrow strips. The space behind one’s closed eyes. The sentence not written in a letter. The half-second before answering a question.
“You asleep?” Jake whispered.
“Yes.”
“Trials Thursday.”
“I know.”
“We’ll smash it.”
“Probably.”
“Not probably.”
“All right.”
“We will.”
I could have said something sensible: that the pitch would be heavy, that Hale would try to make us lose shape, that Holsworth liked strength through the middle but might forgive it if the passing was quick, that possible did not mean promised. Instead I said all right because Jake did not want analysis in the dark. He wanted agreement, or perhaps company inside his certainty.
I gave him that.
Then I said his name.
“Jake?”
“What?”
“Thanks earlier.”
“For what?”
“With Hale.”
“Oh. That.”
“Yes. That.”
“He’s a prat.”
“Yes.”
“So.”
There was no way to explain the size of it without making it smaller. He had corrected Hale about Reading. He had stepped in front of insult as if insult were a ball he could take on the chest and bring down. He had stopped when I touched his sleeve. None of this was heroic. That mattered. Heroics embarrass the person rescued. Small loyalties are easier to live with.
“Still,” I said.
The rain went on.
Across from me, his shape turned toward the window. I could not see his face properly. Only the suggestion of it when the corridor light thinned under the door. Eight beds, eight boys, a term beginning. Somewhere beyond the house wall, the bell house waited to resume its authority in the morning.
I thought of my mother’s hand brushing invisible lint from my shoulder. I thought of the card in my blazer pocket, still there, absurdly carried back into the place from which it had been sent away. I thought of Jake saying you should have come, as if wanting a thing and being able to have it were neighbouring countries with an open border.
Mostly, though, I thought of the moment on the steps when I saw him coming with his trunk, bright with cold and full of Austria, and felt something in me answer too quickly.
I had no name for that.
There were plenty of names at St Cormac’s. Boards full of them. Registers, team sheets, punishment books, chapel lists, stitched labels in collars, fathers’ names, house names, saints’ names, dead boys’ names in stone. The school believed naming a thing gave it order.
I was not sure order was always mercy.
The corridor light went out. Darkness made the room honest for half a minute, then ordinary again.
I turned toward the wall and kept my breathing even until I heard Jake shift once, then settle. Only then did I let myself reach under the folded blazer at the side of the bed and touch the edge of the postcard in the pocket, not taking it out, not reading it, just confirming it was there.
Snow brilliant. You’d die. Jake.
It was a foolish thing to keep.
So I kept it.

essays.title: Prologue - The Years Between
essays.body:
In 2026, St Cormac’s College looked, from a distance, almost innocent.  The drones used for the school prospectus rose above the Pang Valley on a clear October morning and found the place exactly as generations of parents had wanted to imagine it: chapel tower, cloister walk, playing fields, copper beech trees, pale stone touched by weather, the low red roofs of the old dormitory block, and beyond them the newer glass buildings reflecting a clean, corrected sky. 

The chapel bell still rang across the quadrangle. The war memorial still stood where it had stood since 1921. The names were still read in November. The boys — and now girls, though the older brochures would never have believed it — still wore blazers for formal occasions and sang in Latin on feast days when the chaplain thought he could persuade them.  The school website spoke fluently of care.  Safeguarding. Transparency. Inclusion. Pastoral excellence. Diversity of need. Student voice. Independent reporting channels. Trauma-informed practice. The words sat in neat blue tabs beneath a photograph of smiling sixth formers carrying folders across the lawn.

There were policies now for everything. Policies for phones, for bullying, for child protection, for intimate care, for staff conduct, for whistleblowing, for consent, for online safety, for complaints. Visitors signed in at reception and wore lanyards the colour of warning. Monks no longer moved alone through dormitory corridors at night. Housemasters were trained, audited, supervised. The old punishments had become museum pieces. The punishment book, if it still existed, was either in an archive box or a cupboard no one mentioned during tours.

Parents liked the policies. They liked the glass. They liked the girls in the sixth form, the new science centre, the music scholarships, the bursary language, the sense that tradition had been tamed and made safe for modern use.  And perhaps it had.  That was the generous view.  The less generous view was that St Cormac’s had learned, like many old institutions, how to survive being found out.

It had been founded in 1878, on a wooded rise above the Pang Valley, not far from Reading and the old Berkshire roads. Its first prospectuses called it “a child of recusant England, born late, but from ancient stock,” which was the kind of sentence the school loved because it made lateness sound like destiny. The college had not been old, not really. Victorian brick and Catholic ambition had done most of the work. But behind it stood a deeper inheritance: English Catholicism after exclusion, Benedictine patience, the desire to make boys into men who would be obedient without seeming servile, polished without seeming vain, devout without seeming foreign.  Its motto was *In silentio robur*.  In silence, strength.

On the honours boards, the motto looked noble. It suggested restraint, courage, discipline, prayer. It belonged naturally above lists of captains, scholars, prefects, dead officers, abbots, headmasters, and boys who had gone on to become barristers, priests, civil servants, soldiers, surgeons, and once, though the school made too much of it, a minor poet whose collected work was available in the library but seldom borrowed.

In practice, the motto did more complicated work.  Silence could mean reverence before Mass. It could mean the hush after Compline when the chapel lamps were put out and the whole building seemed to breathe in stone. It could mean the held attention of a class translating Virgil, the quiet of snow over the pitches, the minute before a penalty, the pause before a headmaster spoke. It could also mean: do not say.

Do not say what you saw.
Do not say what you felt.
Do not say what the master did.
Do not say why the boy changed.
Do not say why the mother came.
Do not say why the friend was sent away.

Do not say what happened in the bathroom, in the office, in the dormitory, in the car on the way home, in the chapel where the candles burned as if innocence were a matter of lighting. By 2026, that distinction could be written down.  In 1986, it could not.  That is one of the things that must be understood before this story begins. Not excused. Understood.

The boys in this book did not live in a world that gave them the right words. They had Latin before they had language for themselves. They could conjugate verbs of loving and hating, parse a line of Catullus, learn the difference between sin and temptation, between mortal and venial, between obedience and pride. They could recite prayers. They could name Roman battles. They could tell you who scored against Alderton in the ’84 cup final and which master still used the cane and which house had the best view of the cricket square.

But they could not say trauma.
They could not say grooming.
They could not say safeguarding.
They could not say coercion.

They could not say shame, except as something deserved.  They could not say gay as a possibility of ordinary life. Not at St Cormac’s. Not in that decade. Not under that roof, beneath that motto, among boys trained to hear softness as danger and silence as proof of character.

The 1980s did not arrive at St Cormac’s all at once. They seeped in through newspapers in the common room, through fathers’ voices, through jokes in changing rooms, through assemblies about discipline and standards, through the television images boys glimpsed on exeat weekends before returning to a school that still preferred bells to clocks.  Outside, the country was loud.

There were missiles at Greenham Common and women linking arms at the fences. There were arguments about unions, pits, police horses, loyalty, treachery, and what kind of nation Britain intended to be. There was famine on television and pop stars singing beneath stadium lights. There was a ferry that would later go down because doors had been left open. There was a storm waiting in the weather, though no one knew it yet. There was the language of strength everywhere: strong government, strong currency, strong families, strong boys.

There was also fear.  It came folded into newspapers and spoken over breakfast tables. It came in headlines about disease, corruption, permissiveness, moral decay. It came dressed as concern for children. It came as disgust. It came as jokes. It came as warnings. It came as the sudden hardening of adults when certain words were mentioned. It came as the knowledge that to be suspected of one kind of desire was to be reduced to it completely.

For a boy at St Cormac’s in 1986, desire was not identity. It was evidence.  A look could be evidence. A letter. A notebook. A hand held half a second too long. An attachment. A rumour. A nickname. A silence.
The school had its own vocabulary for these things. It did not always need the brutal words the boys used among themselves. Adult language was smoother, and therefore more dangerous. An unhealthy attachment.  A particular friendship.  Emotional irregularity.  A poor influence. Moral danger. Not quite a good mixer.  Needs hardening up.

The words were soft enough to pass across a desk. They could be written in a report. They could be spoken to a parent in a carpeted room beside a crucifix and a tray of cooling tea. They could sound, to a frightened mother, like care.  That is another thing that must be understood.  Harm does not always announce itself as cruelty. Sometimes it enters dressed as responsibility. Sometimes it uses the language of protection. Sometimes the people who do the most damage are certain they are preventing something worse.

By the time the events of this story took shape, St Cormac’s had already been many schools.

It had been a small Victorian Catholic college for the sons of families who wanted English polish without Anglican formation. It had been a cold-water, Latin-and-football place where boys learned obedience before breakfast. It had been a school of war memorials and black ties, where the dead were read aloud so the living would understand the uses expected of them. It had been a place of monks and lay masters, of confession and cricket, of feast days, house colours, scholarship boys, old Catholic names, and new middle-class money.

In the 1950s it had seemed secure. In the 1960s it had begun, quietly, to change. In the 1970s it had survived by admitting more day boys, more non-Catholic families, more sons of accountants, pilots, engineers, estate agents, and men who believed school fees could lift a child across a class boundary if the child learned quickly enough how not to show gratitude.

By the 1980s, it had become a place suspended between two eras. The world outside was accelerating. St Cormac’s was tightening. Its old certainties had not vanished. They had become defensive. The school still believed in polish, house loyalty, Latin tags, corporal correction, controlled affection, competitive sport, and the idea that boys were made, not merely educated. The cane still existed. So did the ledger. So did the dormitory inspections, the prefects, the unspoken ranking of families, the careful distinction between boys whose fathers had been there and boys whose mothers had made sacrifices no one was polite enough to count.

It was not, in its own mind, a cruel place. This matters because cruel places are too easy. St Cormac’s could be beautiful. Many boys loved it. Some were saved by it, or believed they were. It gave structure to the lonely, ambition to the uncertain, ritual to the grieving, confidence to those born expecting it, and a borrowed confidence to those clever enough to imitate. It could produce friendships of startling loyalty. It could make a boy feel chosen by history, held inside something older than himself.

It could also mistake endurance for health.
It could mistake silence for strength.
It could mistake fear for respect.

And once a school has made those mistakes for long enough, it no longer needs villains in every room. The building begins to do some of the work by itself.  The story that follows concerns boys who entered that building before they were old enough to know what it would ask of them.  One came from inheritance: old photographs, old expectations, a father’s name already lodged in the walls. He understood fields, bodies, movement, pressure, the clean logic of a ball played into space. He did not understand the life forming in him where language should have been.

One came on a narrower road: scholarship, vigilance, a mother’s hope folded too tightly around him, the habit of reading rooms because rooms could turn. He noticed hands, pauses, hems, shoes, accents, laughter arriving late. He learned early that belonging was never given whole.  One came bright, quick, funny, too alive to hide properly. He loved words because words promised order. Latin gave him forms for contradiction. *Odi et amo.* I hate and I love. At first it was a line from a poem, clever enough to make other boys smile. Later it became something else.

There were adults too, though not all of them understood they were part of the story.  A mother who loved her son and selected the wrong truth.  A monk who knew the power of being trusted.  A father who believed reputation was a kind of weather: unpleasant when it turned, but survivable if one stayed indoors.  A grieving man on a touchline who would one day say plainly what others had wrapped in silence.  And there was the school itself.

The school rang the bell. The school polished the floor. The school recorded punishments. The school sang the psalm. The school separated boys. The school wrote references. The school carried rumours in the mouths of those too young to understand what they were carrying. The school forgot selectively, which is to say it remembered what protected it.  In 2026, a visitor walking through St Cormac’s might struggle to imagine it.

The reception area would smell of coffee and new carpet, not wax and damp wool. The safeguarding posters would be visible from the entrance. A girl in games kit might cross the quad without anyone finding this remarkable. A boy might text his mother from beneath the cloister and receive an answer before the bell for lunch. A teacher might notice a withdrawn pupil and enter a concern into a system before the end of the day. A word like abuse would no longer have to fight its way into the room.

This is progress.  It is not resurrection.  The past does not disappear because the language improves. It waits in altered buildings. It sits behind plaques. It survives in euphemism, in loyalty, in the strange tenderness old boys feel for places that hurt them, in the official histories that mention reforms without naming what required reform. It remains in photographs where everyone is smiling because the shutter asked them to. It remains in the gap between what happened and what was recorded.

By 2026, St Cormac’s could say the right things.
In 1986, it taught boys not to say the true ones.

This story begins there: before the policies, before the lanyards, before the glass reception, before children carried phones in their pockets like lifelines, before schools learned to speak the language of care with fluency and fear.

It begins when letters took days.
When a closed door was still a closed door.
When a boy could change before everyone’s eyes and the adults could call it moodiness, insolence, softness, sin.
When two friends could stand close enough to understand everything and still lack the one word that might have saved them from misunderstanding it.
It begins in the years when silence was not empty.
It was full.

And it demanded payment.

essays.title: Moral Injury
essays.body:
Moral injury is the wound left when a person commits, enables, fails to prevent, or is made complicit in an act that violates one or more of their deepest values. It is not merely guilt. It is guilt with identity attached. It is shame with a memory. It is the sense that some private court inside the self has reached its verdict, and that no later kindness, apology, success, or suffering can quite overturn it.
The injury becomes more severe when the offending act is not experienced as a temporary lapse, but as evidence of something permanent. The person is not only forced to think, I did something wrong. They are forced toward the more corrosive thought: the part of me that did it is also me. At that point the conflict is no longer between good and evil in some clean moral theatre. It is between two parts of the same person, each claiming authenticity. The value that was betrayed still lives. So does the motive, weakness, fear, desire, obedience, cowardice, ambition, or hunger that betrayed it. Healing then becomes difficult not because the person lacks conscience, but because conscience itself has become a place of torment.
The classic boogeyman is easier to understand. He is the psychopath, the monster without remorse, the one who can do unspeakable things and apparently feel nothing. He is the severed head in the fridge, the battered corpse left for a dog walker, the bag of remains, the obscene trophy mailed to the family. He terrifies because he seems to stand outside ordinary humanity. He does not ask to be forgiven. He does not appear to recognise the need.
But there is another kind of danger.
What of the person who does feel guilt? What of the one who knows, at some level, that a line has been crossed, but cannot bear the knowledge cleanly? What of the person whose remorse does not lead to confession, repair, or restraint, but instead ferments into secrecy, self-pity, rage, numbness, or further harm? Such a person may be more difficult to see clearly. He may weep. He may pray. He may speak movingly of morality. He may despise himself in private and still destroy others in public. He may even believe, with real sincerity, that he is suffering more deeply than those he has harmed.
That is where moral injury becomes morally dangerous: not in the wound itself, but in what the wounded person does to escape feeling it.
The psychopath frightens us because he seems inhuman. The morally injured wrongdoer frightens us because he is not. He remains recognisably human. He may love. He may remember. He may have once believed in goodness. He may still believe in it, desperately, even as he violates it. His danger lies partly in that contradiction. He can pass among the ordinary because he is ordinary in many respects. He can be dutiful, articulate, respectable, useful, even tender. He can be someone’s son, teacher, parent, priest, husband, friend.
History has often tried to protect itself by imagining evil as a separate species. After the Nazis, it was tempting to speak as though such men had belonged to a breed apart: monsters without culture, intelligence, tenderness, humour, discipline, or moral vocabulary. But that explanation is too comforting. It lets the rest of humanity stand outside the dock. It allows people to say: that was them, not us.
The more frightening truth is that mass cruelty rarely requires a world populated only by monsters. It requires permission. It requires language. It requires obedience, fear, belonging, humiliation, resentment, careerism, cowardice, and the dulling of moral attention. It requires people who can still recognise right from wrong, but who learn to place that recognition somewhere safely out of reach.
And we have not outgrown this. In recent years we have watched old delusions return in modern dress: conspiracy, tribal certainty, the seduction of grievance, the pleasure of belonging to a righteous crowd, the willingness to deny plain harm when denial protects identity. The danger is not only what people come to believe. It is what they must stop seeing in order to keep believing it.
That is the terrible debt moral injury can leave inside a person: not simply the memory of having done wrong, but the ongoing labour of not fully knowing it. And that labour is often paid by others.

essays.title: Quotes to use somewhere
essays.body:
Key craft note
For the novel, this idea is powerful if you embody it, not explain it too often.
The best St Cormac’s version is not:

“He was morally injured.”

It is:

**A man kneeling in chapel every morning, praying for forgiveness, then choosing silence again by lunchtime because confession would cost him his name.**

That is where the horror lives. Not in the absence of conscience. In conscience made useless by fear.

essays.title: Thomas
essays.body:
The first thing I knew that morning was that Hale was laughing into his pillow.

This was always a bad sign.

Hale had three laughs, arranged in ascending order of danger. There was the ordinary laugh, which meant someone had called Brother Anselm “Mother Anselm” by mistake, or that the custard at supper had achieved geological status. There was the silent shoulder laugh, which meant someone was about to be in trouble but had not yet discovered it. And then there was the pillow laugh, which meant the trouble had already happened and was lying somewhere in the dormitory, possibly me.

I opened one eye.

The ceiling was still there. Whitewashed, cracked above Cartwright’s bed, damp-stained above mine, with the little brown mark near the beam that looked like Africa if Africa had lost Madagascar in a fight. The bell had not gone. Grey light sat against the windows. Someone’s sock hung from the radiator like a surrendered flag.

Hale made a noise like a kettle being strangled.

“What?” I said.

No one answered.

This was also a bad sign.

There were eight beds in St Aelred’s lower dormitory, though “beds” gives the wrong idea. They were iron-framed instruments of character formation, designed, I think, by a man who believed boys ought to sleep as little as possible in order to leave more time for Latin and moral improvement. Mine was third from the door, which meant I was far enough from the draught to survive winter but close enough to be inspected first if Brother Declan came in.

Across from me, Pritchard was sitting up with both hands pressed over his mouth. Cartwright had pulled his blanket up to his nose. Naylor, who had the face of a farm boy and the conscience of a pirate, was pointing.

At me.

Not at my face.

Lower.

I looked.

There are moments in a boy’s life when the soul attempts to leave the body by the nearest available exit. Mine tried for both ears at once.

My pyjama trousers, which I distinctly remembered tying with a bow of decent moral firmness the night before, had migrated south during the night. Not catastrophically. Not indecently. But enough to reveal that, while the rest of Thomas Ellery was still asleep, a small and deeply disloyal part of the empire had raised the morning standard.

“Oh, brilliant,” I said.

That finished Hale completely. He buried his face in the pillow and thumped the mattress with one fist.

Naylor whispered, “Ellery’s flying colours.”

Pritchard said, “Shut up, he’ll wake the whole house.”

“You’ve woken the whole house,” I said, trying to retrieve the situation, the pyjamas, and my dignity in one movement. I managed the pyjamas. The other two remained somewhere on the floor.

Cartwright, who was usually pale and priestly and looked as if he had been assembled from milk and guilt, said, “It was like reveille.”

“That is a military bugle call,” I said. “Not a suitable term.”

“It was upright,” said Naylor.

“Lots of things are upright. Candlesticks are upright. Brother Anselm’s spine is upright. The chapel tower is upright.”

“The chapel tower hasn’t got rabbits on its pyjamas,” Hale said into the pillow.

I looked down. This was true. My mother had sent the pyjamas from home. They were blue, with small white rabbits on them, because she had bought them when I was eleven and under the impression that clothes were chosen by mothers according to a private system unrelated to age, taste, or survival. I had meant to throw them away. I had also meant to become good at cricket and stop biting my nails. Life is full of unfinished projects.

“Those are hares,” I said. “Distinctly different animal. Longer ears. More tragic expression.”

“Not the only thing with longer—”

“Finish that sentence,” I said, “and I shall translate you into Latin incorrectly for the rest of term.”

Naylor grinned. “You can translate that?”

“Of course I can. The Romans had everything. Roads, baths, aqueducts, enormous public embarrassment.”

Hale came up for air. “What’s Latin for it, then?”

“There isn’t one word,” I said, because I did not know and preferred not to admit it. “Latin is more elegant. It would be a phrase. Something about an ill-timed standard.”

“Standard!” said Pritchard, and collapsed sideways.

This was how the dormitory began chanting, very quietly, because even rebellion at St Cormac’s observed the rules of volume before seven o’clock:

“Stan-dard. Stan-dard. Stan-dard.”

I sat upright, which was a mistake, as everyone immediately found this unbearably funny.

“I hope you all fail Common Entrance retrospectively,” I said.

“You can’t fail it retrospectively,” Cartwright said.

“You can if I mark it.”

The door handle moved.

Eight boys became corpses.

The door opened six inches and Brother Anselm put his head in. He wore his morning expression, which was not an expression so much as the absence of forgiveness. His hair, what little there was of it, stood up at the back in three white tufts. This made him look less like a monk and more like an elderly chick who had taken a vow of silence and then regretted it.

“What is this noise?”

No one spoke.

Brother Anselm looked along the beds. Pritchard had achieved unnatural stillness. Hale was purple. Naylor had buried himself under the blanket, which was suspicious because Naylor never hid from anything unless it was work.

I had my sheet clutched to my chest like a dying heroine in a melodrama.

Brother Anselm’s eyes settled on me.

“Ellery.”

“Yes, Brother.”

“Are you ill?”

“No, Brother.”

“Then why are you sitting like that?”

There are several possible answers to this question. None of them improves a situation.

“I was thinking, Brother.”

“At half past six?”

“Yes, Brother.”

“About what?”

Hale made a tiny squeak.

“Mortality,” I said.

Brother Anselm stared at me.

This was not, in fairness, entirely a lie. I had been thinking that I might die.

“Mortality,” he repeated.

“Yes, Brother.”

“You may contemplate mortality after washing. All of you up. Bell in seven minutes. And I do not want a herd of cattle on the stairs.”

He withdrew.

The door closed.

No one moved.

Then Hale whispered, “Mortality,” and the dormitory fell apart.

By the time the bell went, my name had altered. I was no longer Ellery. I was Standard. This was better than some alternatives and worse than all forms of silence. At St Cormac’s, a nickname could arrive faster than measles and lasted longer. A boy in the year above had once sneezed during Benediction and was still called Gloria, because the sneeze had come precisely after *Gloria Patri*. There was another boy called Moose for reasons no one remembered, including Moose.

I dressed with great care and my back to the room.

“Modest now, is he?” said Naylor.

“I have always been modest,” I said. “My modesty is one of my chief qualities.”

“Second after architecture,” said Hale.

“That joke lacks proportion.”

“So did you.”

Pritchard made the strangled kettle noise this time.

I tied my school tie too tightly and had to do it again. My face had gone hot, which annoyed me more than the joke. There is nothing worse than blushing when people want you to blush. It is like handing ammunition to an enemy and helping him load.

But it was funny. That was the worst of it. I could see that it was funny. If it had happened to Hale, I would have been useless for twenty minutes. If it had happened to Naylor, I would have composed a hymn.

*Surge, vexillum*, I thought.

Rise, banner.

No. Absolutely not. Never write that down.

Downstairs, the corridor smelt of polish, damp wool, and boys who had washed parts of themselves in water cold enough to discourage sin. The house noticeboard had yesterday’s football teams pinned to it, the paper curling at one corner. Jake Verity’s name was on the First XI trial list, even though he was too young really, because Jake Verity had the sort of legs masters trusted before they trusted his character. Marcus Webb’s name was not on any list. Marcus had arrived with books wrapped in brown paper and a face that noticed things before deciding whether to admit it.

He was standing by the boot-room door when we came down, doing up his cuff. He looked up as the dormitory passed.

“Morning,” he said.

“Careful,” said Hale. “Ellery’s already had one.”

Everyone laughed again.

Marcus looked at me.

The thing about Marcus was that he did not laugh until he knew where the blade was. His eyes moved from Hale to Naylor to me, then away, politely. Not innocent. Worse. Merciful.

“Latin test today?” he said.

“Yes,” I said. “The Gallic Wars. Death would be kinder.”

“That may be what Caesar thought.”

“Caesar thought very highly of Caesar.”

“So do most conquerors.”

This was why I liked Marcus. He answered properly. Most boys only waited for their turn to say a louder thing.

Jake came in from the side passage with mud already on one sock, which was impressive at half past six and perhaps a school record. His tie was crooked, his hair wet, his shirt half out. He looked as if he had been invented by a games master during a fever.

“What’s funny?” he said.

“No,” I said.

Hale said, “Standard.”

Jake looked blank.

“Don’t ask,” Marcus said.

Jake looked at Marcus, then at me. “All right.”

And there it was.

Only a little thing. A nothing thing. A boy not asking because another boy had told him not to. But I saw Marcus see it too, and then pretend not to. His fingers were still on his cuff, though the cuff was already done.

I thought: oh.

Then I thought: don’t be stupid.

Then I thought, because the mind is a traitor and mine worse than most: *odi et amo*.

I hate and I love.

Catullus had the advantage of being dead. No one could flick porridge at him for saying things like that.

We went into breakfast under the portraits of old headmasters, all of them looking down with the same expression, as if the dining hall had disappointed them personally. Brother Declan stood near the serving hatch with his hands folded into his sleeves. He saw everything without appearing to look. That was his trick. Some masters watched you like policemen. Brother Declan watched you like a question.

“Ellery,” he said as I passed.

I stopped.

“Yes, Brother.”

“Latin after chapel. Bring your exercise book.”

“Yes, Brother.”

His eyes rested on my face for half a second too long.

Behind me, Naylor whispered, very softly, “Standard bearer.”

I did not laugh. Not because it wasn’t funny. It was. Horribly.

I did not laugh because Brother Declan was still looking at me, and the joke, which had been warm and stupid and ours upstairs, suddenly felt like something left out in the cold.
